Intelligence from Constantinople, to the 27th ult., has been received by the Tagus. It seems that in several towns of Asia, manifestations have been made hostile to the reforms recently decreed ; at Aidin, especially, the Christians have been mal-treated. It was said that the cavalry repressed a disturbance by the Turkish population at Ismid. The followingisan authentic list of the atrocities which the Austrians have committed during the short interval alone I of twenty-five days in the single city of Bucharest: In the first week of this short period, eighteen assassinations were committed by the Austrians, and proved on evidence. On the 23rd of February they killed in broad day-light, in the Cotzotcheni quarter, three men who had lodged a complaint against the murderers tor an act they had previously committed. In the night of the 26th they killed three other men in the Street of the Tanners for the mere sake of a loaf of sugar which they had at first tried to take from them by brute force. The assassins of the first three victims are known to the Austrian commander, but, notwithstanding this, no proceedings have been taken against them. On the 24th they cut off the arms and legs of a poor fellow and threw the mutilated body into the Dumbovitza. On that same day, about nine þÿo clock in the evening, they killed in the middle of the street a man because he tried to protect his wife and prevent her from being carried off by them. On the 25th, in the afternoon, three Austrian soldiers,

in the presence of several of their officers, killed a man in the Tchismedgi garden. It is affirmed that the Turkish plenipotentiaries demanded of Russia an indemnity for the expenses of the war, and for damages sustained through repeated invasions of the Principalities by Russia. These latter damages, it is

said, have been frequently admitted by the Russian government, which has promised reparation, but hitherto has not kept its word. This demand the Russian plenipotentiaries rejected. The evacuation of the Principalities has not been obtained without difficulties : nothing short but ot a threatening of a casus belli could decide the Austrian Government lo the withdrawal of the army from the Danubian provinces.

THE CRIMEA AND SOUTHERN ASIA. The evacuation of the Crimea appears (to have received its commencement. The Paris papers contain accounts from that peninsula to the 22nd. The French Intendance had chartered a number of merchant-vessels for the conveyance of stores from that country, and a number of articles which were to be first shipped had already been sent to Ivamiesch. The health of the troops continued to improve. The French army will return from the Crimea in bodies of 20,000, with corresponding materiel. About six months It will be occupied in the evacuation. will begin in May, and last over October.
AUSTRIA. The Austrian army in the Principalities will quit these provinces. The withdrawal of the troops has already commenced.

MARTIAL LAW IN FARM A This small State still continues in the same condition of alarm on the part of the Government. All letters from Piedmont are opened by the authorities, and are afterwards sent to their addresses closed with the seal of tho military commandant. Arrests still continue ; among them may be mentioned those of Count Hoiardi, a merchant of the name of Uambaro, and Dr. Tebaldi. It is rumoured that the military commission has discovered a general plot against the Government ; that several of the persons arrested were provided with forged passports ; and that the place whore such passports were prepared has been discovered.

The Late Lord Raglan and the War in the Crimea. þÿ As peace gives leisure for inquiry, so does it clear up many misrepresentations about the war. The English army, which our journalists delighted to disparage, will come out with a higher reputation when the truth is known. It is now ascertained that, at the battle of the Alma, not 6,000 Russian troops were, left in Sebastopol. The Russian Plenipotentiaries have stated this at the Conference. Lady Raglan has a letter in her possession, proving that Lord Raglan sent to St. Arnaud when the battle was gained, to say that he was pushing on to enter Sebastopol, and that the French Commander-in- Chief refused to support him, and required him to move on Commander llad Lord Raglan been to Balaklava. of both armies, we would have been in Sebastopol at the very opening of the campaign. We are further in a condition to state that four times over Lord Raglan ordered the bombardment of Odessa, when he found the enemy drawing strength from it. The order was telegraphed to Paris, and four times Napoleon prohibited it. We can also state that at the battle of the Tchernaya, the English General sent to the French Commander to say that he would seize the bridge over the river, and intercept the retreat of 25,000 Russians, who the Russian Plenipotentiaries now say were completely disorganized. The French Commander again refused the offer, and allowed the Russians to escape. These matters must he cleared up.

A telegraph despatch þÿ Madrid, says : from on Tuesday last, The day before yesterday (April 6) an insurrection broke out in Valencia, for which the conscription was the pretext. The authorities got the better of it. Tranquility appears to have been re-established. Government has given the strictest orders to declare the province in a state of seige, and to put in force the law of the 17th of April, 1821 , against the disturbers of order, without delay. All measures have been taken for repressing rigorously and instantaneously any attempt at disorder, wherever it may occur. Madrid is tranquil, as are all the provinces from which news have been received. This is, therefore, the fuel for warm latitudes, as well as warm seasons ; and this conclusion is borne out, by the stronger tendency to its production in its various forms, in the warmer temperate and torrid regions. COMMUNICATIONS. Mr. Editor, þÿ Being convinced that nineteuths of the inhabitants of this island are not aware that there is at this moment pending in the Colonial Council, a question the most vital in importance to their interests that has as yet been brought before that body, it is hut right, that through the medium of tho press, tiiat great organ of public enlightenment, they should know that our gracious sovereign, who has so nobly granted a constitution to his European subjects, has now required to bo informed through the medium of tho Colonial Council, whether his subjects in his colonies, wish to be governed by his Imperial state council, or by the Diet of Copenhagen, or whether they would profer to govern themselves. As it is difficult to bo supposed that any disinterested and sane man will hesitate in his preference of self-government, you arc now, inhabitants of St. Croix, seriously called upon to throw off your wonted listlessness and inattention to the general welfare, in which every man is deeply concerned, and by a respectful but energetic petition, make the members of the Colonial Council, and through them our most gracious King, unmistakably acquainted with your real prefcrcnoc. Will you hereafter have the'taunt, the reproach, that when the boon was as it were, placed in the palms of your hands, you were too careless, too apathetic, just to closo your fingers in order to grasp it. If so always remember that the political proclania was issued ; that you would not enter
your claim, and are therefore justly, and perhaps for ever excluded. GRACCHUS St Croix 14th May 1856

THE ENGLISH LUTHERAN CONGRE- GATION AT ST. THOMAS. A numerously signed petition from the above congregation has been presented to the Colonial Council, praying for the speedy appointment of a resident minister. It cannot be denied, as has been remarked on former occasions, that it is singular no minister has been appointed since the death of the last incumbent. There has been a vacancy in that parish during ten months. It was certainly desirable that Government had taken the initiative in the matter. Proceeding from the fact, that no nomination has taken place, we must arrive at the conclusion that the subject has not received all the attention it deserves. It is thus evident, that as a last resource the congregation is justified in appealing to the Council for its support, in order to obtain a resident minister. On the recommendation of the Council, Government will, no doubt, take the necessary steps to effect the desired boon. Wo cannot perceive any pecuniary difficulty in the matter, ent of the for as the officiating minister is the pay, fees and emoluments of that recipiliving, which certainly hitherto have been considered sulficient for the support of a resident clergyman, it is apparent that the means are at hand for salarying a resident minister. It will now rest with the Council and Government how speedily the prayer of the petition will be realized. But we cannot, however withhold the remark, that if religious affairs are to be considered as subordinate to pecuniary arrangements, we may then apprehend such a retrogression in re-
ligion and morality as will be injurious and deplorable in the extreme.

RUSSIA The accounts from Warsaw, of the 26th ult., mention that the greatest distress exists there among the poorer classes. The Emperor had been under tho necessity, from official reports sent to him, to order funds from the Imperial treasury to be applied for the immediate relief of tho existing distress. The navigable Pinster Canal, which has been

in course of construction for many years, and is executed for account of the Russian Government, is at length completed, and has just been opened. This canal promises to be of great importance for the internal commerce of Russia, as it allows of uninterrupted communication between the Bug and the Dnieper. The blockade of the Russian ports has had the effect of proving the value of this internal communication, by means of which we have already received from the south ot Russia and through this canal and the river V istula 10,000 quarters of the finest linseed, 12,000 cwt. of tallow, and 15,000 cwt. of hemp, a great part of which has been already shipped to England. For tho greater facilitation of this trade, a service of steam-tugs is being organised by the Russian Government, which will be completed in the course of this summer.

A Ruse A letter from the Crimea shows how a Sardinian soldier contrived to fill his purse during the conference between the generals respecting the armistice : " During the interview, some Zouaves were on the banks of the Tchernaya, with bottles in their hands, signalling invitations to the Russians to come and partake. Rut how was this to be done ? The Traktir Bridge was reserved for the generals, in order to prevent a crowd there, and the oflicers and soldiers, ardently wishing to cross the river to the Russians, were in despair of being able to do so. Suddenly a stout Sardinian soldier offered for a sou per head to pass to the other side any one who would mount on his shoulders. lie ' One instantly cheap and, when landed on the oppo- was sou !' exclaimed every one ; ' how " overwhelmed with orders.

site bank, they warmly thanked him, rallying him a little on the cheapness ol his charge, lie replied with a malicious smile, which no one understood ; but they afterwards discovered its meaning. After the interview, all who had passed the river on the soldier's back wished to return to the left side by the same road They called to the aquatic warrior, and made signs to him to approach ; but he replied, laughing in a most provoking manner, that the water was cold, and that he was afraid of the rheumatism. In brief it was necessary to pay him what he asked. They treated the matter as pleasantly as they could, and in a few minutes the soldier found himself in possession of a good round sum. Ouo Fallacies become New Facts, þÿ It has long been a question whether the sun's rays can render a needle magnetic. Morichini, Mrs. Somerville and Baumgartner have cheifiy investigated the matter. It ocurred to Reichenbach that the sun's rays might play a part in the result of his investigations, and the idea acquired some probability, when the influence exerted by the moon on certain nervous disorders þÿ an influence well known and undeniable þÿ was taken into consideration. The first sunny day was accepted for trying the experiment. The room being darkened, a copper wire, thirty feet long, was placed in the hands of Mdlle. Maix, and, when her hand was accustomed to the contact, the other end was put out of the window affixed to a copper plate, nine inches square, and exposed to the sun. No sooner was this done than he was saluted by a cry of pleasure from the sick couch. The moment the sun's rays fell upon the plate, a powerful manifestation of the well-known force was felt, as a pleasurable feeling rising through the arm to the head, which the patient compared to the fresh air of a fine May morning. The end of the wire was also luminous, with a flame from nine to twelve inches in height. A glass of water, placed in the sun's rays for 20 minutes, and handed by one of the weakest female hands, acted as strongly as if magnetised by the large horse-shoe magnet of nine bars, capable of supporting 801bs. Another experiment was with the spec trum, to see whether, in all the rays,

the crystalline resided in different degrees. A spectrum was thrown on the wall, and Mdlle. Maix holding in her hand one end of a copper wire, the other end was moved along the spectrum from tint to tint, without her knowing what was done. Many repeated experiments, which gave uniform results, showed that green, and still more, yellow, were especially the seat of the delightful sunny feeling of re freshing coolness. In the violet ray, and beyond it, the patient found the seat of that peculiar disagreeable sensation with which she was familiar in the magnets (that is, of the pure magnetic or iron attracting power, not possessed by crystals or the human hand) ; this was perceived also by several other highly sensitive patients. The violet is the very part of the spectrum where Morichini and Mrs. Somcrville succeeded in magnetising steel This observation adds some weight to the researches of these experimentali/.ers, which are not generally admitted,

The following is a Copy of a Petition front the Inhabitants of this Island now in I course of signature, to be laid before the ; Colonial Council, on the all-important subject of obtaining the management of our own internal affairs, without which we can never hope to effect a salutary retrenchment in the enormous expenses which at present are crushing out the vital energies of this community. We deem it superflous to recommend this petition to the serious consideration of the people of this Island ; the subject matter of the document speaks for itself, we only regret that time will not permit to have a similar one circulated in j the sister Island of St. Thomas, which should be done if possible. There may be some little inaccuracies in this petition which however do not weaken or affect its import ; but this arises from the want of proper publicity which should be given to ( all matters concerning the public interest brought before what was intended, we conceive, to be a popular assembly representing the voice of the people. We conceive, that no þÿ þÿdisinterested or þÿ þÿsane man will neglect to sign this document. If we neglect now to express our feelings

and opinions on a subject which so urgently demands that expression from us, we shall hereafter have no right to complain. A copy remains at Mr. G Behaþÿgen sstore in Bassin for signature, and one at Mr. þÿRobinson store s in West 'End. B. N. To the Honorable the Colonial Council, in Council Assembled. The humble Petition of the undersigned inhabitants of St. Croix, Sheweth : That, whereas it has come to our knowledge that, His Gracious Majesty the King, has signified his Royal Will to the Honorable Colonial Council, desiring to be informed through your Honorable Assembly, as representatives of the people of these Islands, whe- ! ther his subjects residing in this distant portion of his Dominions, should wish to be governed by his Imperial State Council, or by the Diet, or whether they would prefer to govern and manage their own internal affairs þÿ And that at this moment, this all important subject is under discussion in your Honorable Assembly. That we consider it would be a dereliction of duty on our part did we not come forward at this time and make our sentiments and feelings unmistakably known on this vital question, and forcibly to manifest to the Colonial Council, and through them, to His Majesty the King, that we are not insensible to the great advantages which we believe would, in due time, flow to these Coionies from the possession of the right to manage our own internal affairs. That we look upon the right and power of selfgovernment in all enlightened and civilised communi-

ties as an inestimable blessing, without which no people or community can be really prosperous and happy. That the History of all Colonies very distant from the Mother-country, or governing power, proves the inability of the latter to direct and govern the internal affairs of the former, with just advantages to their interests, with whose peculiarities and wants they, in the Mother-country, must be at best but very imperfectly acquainted. That we believe no body of men in Copenhagen, even if well disposed towards us, can direct and govern our internal affairs wi h the same advantage to us as we could ourselves, more particularly by the Diet, which, judging from the remarks occasionally enunciated by some members of that assembly, we must bold the opinion, displays not only much ignorance regarding us, but proves that no sympathy or friendly feeling towards us exists in that political þÿbody vide a late speech delivered in the Diet by a Mr. l.chniann. That among the paramount advantages which, we are convinced are to be derived to the interests and welfare of these Colonies from seit-governinent, we would respectfully mention, the power and ability to retrench the enormous and unnecessary expences of these Colonies, thereby enabling the reduction of Taxes, which at present press so heavily on the community. To raise up and foster institutions suited to our peculiar and local wants, embracing more particularly the extension and more efficient organization ol schools, the care and proper support of our clergy and

churches, in order to afford religions instruction to all classes of people in all parts of the Island þÿ particularly to the country Labourers þÿ wants which at. present are so seriously felt. To establish and maintain a stronger Police force. To have but one Treasury for the separate Budget for these Colonies. To reduce receipt ot all Taxes, dues, and imposts, and to nave our a present postal Law of its cumbrous dimensions and , make it suitable to our position and wants. To organise a respectable Militia, which would materially aid in diminishing an enormous item in our expences, and which we beg leave to state, we believe, could be achieved without much difficulty. That we wish it to be clearly understood that we do not desire to interfere with the judicature of the Danish Law, much less do we wish our connexion with the Monarchy at all weakened. That we would wish to enlarge much more on this subject did time that permit, and we must remark that, as it is, we fear but a small portion of those who wish to sign this meinoria. will have an opportunity to do so. Finally we entreat your honorable Council to give these our opinions and sentiments all the force in your power, and most particularly do we pray that this Petition may be attached to the final report ol the Committee which has (or may be) appointed to make report on this .subject, and for which, as in duty bound, we shall ever pray. St. Croix 19th May 1856.

The ratification of that all-absorbing topic þÿ The treaty of þÿPeace, after the preliminaries usual on such occasions were carefully observed, had been expected to been signed at Paris before I left St. be exchanged at Paris. The treaty comprises 34 articles, which are too lengthy tor our paper. The first four articles contain the principal items. Those subsequent treat of the territorial settlement, the border line, the navigation of the Danube and the neutrality of the Black Sea. These are the most prominent parts of the Treaty : The Plenipotentiaries, after having exchanged their plenary powers, and ascertained them to be in good and due form, have agreed upon the following Articles : þÿ Article I. From the day of the exchange þÿ of the rat fications of the present treaty, there shall be peace and friendship between his Majesty the Emperor of the French, iter Majesty the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, his Majesty the King of Sardinia, his Majesty the Sultan, of the one part, and his Majesty the Emperor of all the Russias of the other part, as well as between their heirs and successors, their respective States and subjects, in perpetuity. Article 2. þÿ Peace being happily established between their aforesaid Majesties, the territories conquered or occupied by their armies during the war shall be reciprocally evacuated. Special arrangements shall regulate the mode of evacuation, which must be

effected as promptly as possible. Article 3. þÿ H. M. the Emperor of all the Russias engages to restore to II. M. the Sultan the town and citadel of Kars, as well as all the other parts of the Ottoman territory of which the Russian troops are in possession. Article 4. Their Majesties the Emperor of the þÿ French, the Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, the King of Sardinia and the Sultan engage to restore to his Majesty the Emperor of all theRussias, the towns and ports ol Sebastopol Balaklava, Kamiesch, Eupatoria, Kertch.

The same day that the Emperor addressed to his people the manifesto in which he announced the conclusion of peace, lie gave to the army a proof of his satisfaction. He signed an ukase which modifies the statutes of St. George This order, created by Catherine II., and in part reformed by Alexander I , comprises lour classes, a nd an honorary distinction for non-commissioned officers and soldiers. In consideration of the excellent services rendered by the army during the war, and in order to encourage for the future its spirit and bravery, the Emperor has ordered that the mark of distinction granted to the non-commissioned officers and soldiers shall in future also he divided into four classes. The first two will he known by a gold cross, decorated with the picture ot St. George; the third and fourth by a silver cross. For the soldiers of the Mahometan belief, a Russian eagle will replace the cross. The crosses will he worn on ti ribbon attached to the button hole. Every soldier or non-commissioned officer who receives the fourth class of the order shall he entitled to an increase of a third of his pay ; the third class will receive double pay ; and, finally, the first class will enjoy a further increase of half the pay These are very great advantages, of which the army will much approve.

The Treaty justifies the predictions that were made of it. It ends the war between Russia and Turkey ; but takes no account nl the general circumstances of Europe, or of tl« possibilities þÿ not to say the probabilities þÿ of war that exist in other quarters. As a settlement of the disputes between Russia and the Porte, I he Treaty is satisfactory in every respect but one. It does not compel the aggressive Power to pay any portion of the costs of the war which it unrighteously provoked. In every other point of view þÿ considered as a question between those two Powers iu the first instance, and between those two Powers and the rest of Europe in the second þÿ the terms of the Treaty are highly favourable to the Ottoman empire, and to the Allies who took up arms to resist a particular act of aggression. Sebastopol cannot be again rebuilt to overawe Constantinople, and to control the Euxine, without compelling every Power who signed the Treaty to unite with (ireat Britiain, France, and Turkey in levelling it to the ground

No fortresses can be constructed on any portion of the seaboard or littoral of that region, Circassia included. The Russians are to evacuate Kars þÿ the Austrians, Moldavia and Wallachia þÿ and the British, French, and Sardinians, the Crimea, and every portion both of Russian and Turkish territory. After the review of the Russian troops, the Russian General invited Marshal Pelissier, Generals Codrington and Marmora, and several tier in a tent superior and on subaltern officers to a din- j ' the Mackenzie heights. The General continues : þÿ " After a toast proposed by me to the health of the Kmperor of the French, Queen Victoria, and the King of Sardinia, Marshal Pelissier proposed a toast to the health of his Majesty the Emperor and the armies of his Imperial Majesty. In a long speech, he expressed his veneration for his Majesty, and his lively sympathies for our troops. The Empress continues to improve in health, and that of the Imperial Prince is also satisfactory. The programme for the church and baptism is arranged, hut the dates not yet definitively decided on. Her Majesty will shortly remove to St. Cloud, and after the baptism proceed to Biarritz.

A very practical confirmation of the re-establishment of peace, so far as the soldiers are concerned, has been the stoppage of the fid. per diem extra pay, or field allowance, which they have been drawing for some time past. It was ordered to be given so long as the men were in presence of an enemy, and there being no longer any enemy, it now of course ceases. The cessation of this allowance has been notified in the general orders þÿ the stoppage to commence from the date on which the news was received in the Crimea of the treaty having been signed, namely, the 2nd April.

THE DANUB1AN PRINCIPALITIES A despatch from Constantinople states that the Grand Council of the Ottoman Empire has pronounced the deposition of the two Hospodars of Moldavia and Wallachia. The former of these Princes, Gregory Alexander Gliika, had anticipated this measure by recently sending in his resignation ; but the latter, Demetrius Stirbey, clungto power, and to him this will be a heavy blow. While depriving the two Hospodars of office, the Grand Council appointed a Caimacan, or Viceroy, of the Sultan, to govern each of the two provinces, in the name of his Highness, until their reorganisation under the treaty. The Caimacan selected for Wallachia is the Grand Ban Constantine Gliika, and for Moldavia the Grand Logothete Balche. Finally, at the self-same sitting, the Grand Council named as Commissioner of the Porte in the Principalities, and probably as the future representative ot Turkey in the mixed Commission just alluded to, Safet Efl'endi, the present Mustechar ot the Grand Vizier. He is said to be a man of merit.

Commercial relations with France, England, Sardinia, and Turkey are re-established on the old bases. Two merchant vessels, one Austrian and the other Sardinian, entered the port of Odessa on the fith. PERSIAN INTERVENTION IN HERAT. By the Overland Mail we are informed that a Persian army was marching on Herat. This intelligence is interesting 1 in connection with our alliance offensive and defensive, with Dost Mahomed. The movement on Herat must be intended either to support or to destroy the Suddozye Prince Mohammed Yusuf, who three months ago recovered the city by the aid of a Persian force, and professed to hold it as the vassal of Teheran. It is said that the Prince finds himself strong enough to throw off his Persian allegiance and set up for himself; and, if so, of course it is not oaths or obligations that will bind him. But his detection would place him between two fires, for he can expect nothing but hostility at Cabul ; and it is more probable, therefore, that it is in support of its puppet that the Persian Court has dispatched | an army to Herat.

THE RIGHT REVEREND LORD TALBOT. His Lordship, who is on a mission from His Holiness the Pope to inquire into the state and progress of the Catholic Religion in the West Indies, celebrated High Mass in the Catholic Church of Frederiksted on Thursday last (Corpus Christy, ) at 7 o'clock in the morning and administered the Sacrament of Holy Eucharist to 318 persons. At a subsequent Mass which was offered up at 10 o'clock, His Lordship also administered the Sacrament of Confirmation to 90 postulants and delivered a most impressive sermon. At a later period of the day His Lordship inspected the schools attached to the church

and was highly pleased with the advancement of the children. This distinguished personage visited this town on Saturday last. On delivered an eloquent sermon Sunday to a verv he large congregation which had assembled in the Catholic Church. After dwelling lor a considerable time on the duties of man to his Creator and giving striking illustrations from the Bible, he concluded by imploring his people to attend to their religious duties and to obey their superiors, whether civil or ecclesiastical, whom Ood had placed over them. The Revd. Orcini celebrated High Mass, assisted by the Rev. i O'Ryan, parish priest of Frederiksted and the Revd. McNamie, parish priest of this town. Monsieur Chedeville, French Consul at St. Thomas, who is on a visit to this Island, attended Divine Service. Bishop Talbot gave a lecture yesterday morning, after which he proceeded to W est End, thence for St. Thomas en route to Europe.

FACTS AATI SCRAPS. Effective Oratory. þÿ The true use of language is to express, and not, as Talleyrand said, to conceal, our thoughts ; and he is the best writer and speaker who can convey his meaning in the fewest and choicest words. It is a great mistake to suppose that many words make a good style, or that sounding words give power to speech ; they, for the most part, do but weaken it. We may compare the noisy speaker, who culls all the flows of rhetoric wherewith to garnish his discourse, and whose sentences are rounded with the pomp of an inflated oratory, to a shallow and babbling brook, the stony bottom whereof can be discerned through the musical gloss of its waters. Deep streams make no noise, but are self-sustained, concentrated and irresistible in their strength ; and so the great speaker will manifest his superiority by the grandeur of his thoughts rather than the grandiloquence of his language. This is eloquence, and there is none other. Speak always through the head to the heart þÿ for this is the true method ; and depend upon it, the heart can only be reached to any enduring purpose by appeals which are founded in truth and justice. Enthusiastic screams may, for a moment, carry an audience in the whirlwind which they raise ; but reflection returns, and there is an end of such influence. That is the true enthusiasm, when a man kindling with his subject, speaks the words which his thoughts naturally suggest ; for in well-disciplined minds the intellect is ever active and vigilant þÿ even in the

stormy tempests of passion and debate þÿ and restrains within the limits of judicious speech the fiery ebulitions which are prompted by enthusiasm. Sleep. þÿ There is no fact more clearly established in the Physiology of man than this, that the brain expends its energies and itself during the hours of wakefulness, and that these are temperated during sleep ; if the recuperation does not equal the expenditure, the

brain withers þÿ this is insanity. Thus it is that, in early English history, persons who were condemned to death by being prevented from sleeping, always died raving maniacs ; thus it is also that those who are starved to death become insane; the brain is not nourished, and they cannot sleep. The practical inferences are three : þÿ 1st. Those who think most, who do most brain work, " require saved" from necessary sleep is infalli- most sleep. 2nd. That time bly destructive to mind, body and estate. 3rd. Give yourself, your children, your servants, give all that are under you the fullest amount of sleep they will take by compelling them to go to bed at some regular, early hour, and to rise in the morning the moment they awake of themselves, and, within a fortnight, nature, with almost the regularity of the rising sun, will unloose the bonds of sleep the moment enough repose has been secured for the wants of the system. This is the only safe and sufficient rule; and as to the question how much sleep any one requires, each must be a rule for himself ; great Nature will never fail to write it out to the observer, under the regulations just given.

Cato. þÿ If Cicero had too little character, Cato had too much. Public virtue is like gold ; if it is to be current, it must be alloyed. Cato left the alloy out, and cared little whether his coin circulated or not ; all he knew was, that its purity must never be tempered with, and that whoever would not receive it as he tendered it must be corrupt or criminal. He was a good orator, but his oratory was in vain ; he was always ready with advice, but it was advice incapable of being put in practice ; he was esteemed by all, but with an esteem that bore no fruit. Inflexibly and almost savagely austere, he was one of those men whom posterity place in their Valhallas, but whom nations, unless for example's sake, deny admittance to their councils þÿ the most irreproachable of virtuous men, but the most useless.

The Union- Jack. þÿ The British Flag consists of the crosses of St. George, St. Andrew, and St. Patrick, united ; but the etymology of the term " Union- Jack" has never, it is presumed, been explained, for it does not occur " in any lexicon or glossary. The word Union" obviously arose from the event to which the flag owes it origin (the Union of Ireland, in 1801) ; the only difficulty, therefore, is as to the expression "Jack." As the alteration in the banner of St George occurred in the reign ol James I., it may with great probability lie supposed to be a corruption of "Jacques." If, however, this hypothesis be rejected, the following is submitted. English soldiers were formerly accustomed to wear the cross of St. George on their uppergarment ; and as it appears from early writers that the upper dress of a horseman, and, according to others, a coat of mail, was called a " Jack," it admits ol the inference that a small flag containing the cross in question was termed "a Jack," when used at sea ; after the banner, which, more properly speaking, is confined to the field, fell into comparative disuse. The former of these conjectures appears, however, the more probable. þÿ Sir Harris Nicholas. From " Things Not Generally Known."

Before making any proposal, the Danish Government, endeavoured to find a way of solution which at the same time was acceptable to foreign Powers and consistent with þÿDenmark s interests. This double end the Danish Government has only been able to attain by proposing the abolition of the <ound dues for a capital of 35,000,000 i ixdollars Danish money þÿ a sum which scarcely exceeds one-lialfof the capital which, at 4 per cent, interest, represents the yearly income of the Sound dues. Although this arrangement imposes considerable pecuniary sacrifices upon several States, it is the only practicable one, and it must lie kept in mind that the Powers to whose lot the heaviest share would fall are those most interested in the abolition of the Sound dues, as well as in every important European question. In fact, no voice lias been raised against the equity

of þÿDenmark p s roposal and against the moderate views the Danish Government lias taken in this question. Several Powers þÿ as Sweden, Norway, and Rus- <j;, whose share in the capitalization would exceed 7,000,000 silver roubles þÿ' 28,000,0001.) have not hesitated to acto cept it. Others have not whose the call, and England, yet answered interest it seems to he to watch over the independence of Denmark, has declined to enter into the proposed arrangement. It is easily understood that the payment of more than 1 þÿ,000,000/. the proportional share of Great þÿBritain may awaken apprehensions in a constitutional Government ; and no Government can l>e expected to he very inclined to call upon the nation whose interests are committed to their care to pay a similar sum. igencies of the time, without violently making away with old traditions. Turin, May 8. þÿ þÿ The following is a translation of the verbal note presented by the Sardinian Plenipotentiaries to the Ministers of France and England on the 27th ot j March, 1856 At the moment when the glorious forces of the Western Powers lend to assure the benefits ot peace to Europe, the deplorable state of the provinces under the government of the Holy 8ee, and, above all, ot the Legations, calls for the special attention ot the governments of her Hritaunic Majesty and of his Majesty the Emperor of the French. The Legations have been occupied by Austrian troops since 1849. The state of siege and martial law have been in vigour since t hat time without interruption. The Pontifical Government only exists in name, since above its legates an Austrian general takes the title, and exercises the functions of civil and military governor. Nothing evinces that this state of things will terminate, since the Pontifical Government is as convinced of its impotence to preserve public order us in the first days of its restoration, and Austria asks for nothing better than to render her occupation permanent. Here, then, are the farts w hich present themselves ; a deplorable situation existing always in a country nobly peopled, and in which conservative elements abound; impotence of the legitimate Sovereign to govern ; a permanent danger of disorders and anarchy in Central Italy þÿ extension of Austrian dominion in the Peninsula : beyond what the ireaties of 1815 had provided. were The Legations before the French Revolution

under the high sovereignty of the Pope ; but they enjoyed privileges and franchises which rendered them, at least in the internal administration, almost independent. At the same time the clerical dominion was even then so antipathetical that the French army was received in 1796 with enthusiasm. Detached from the Holy Sec by the Treaty of Tolentino, thos-- provinces formed a part of the Republic, afterwards of the kingdom, of Italy until 1814. The organising genius of Napoleon changed their aspect as by enchantment. The French laws, institutions, and administration in a few years developed wealth and civilisation. For this reason, in those provinces, all the traditions, all the sympathies are fixed on that period. The government of Napoleon is the only one that survives in the memory, not. only of enlightened classcss, but of the people. His me-

3 U 2L A T )i 3 mory recalls an impartial justice, a strong administration, a state altogether of prosperity, of riches, and of military greatness. At the Congress of Vienna they hesitated a long time about replacing the Legations under the government of the Pope. The statesmen who sat there, although preoccupied with the thought of re-establishing the ancient order of things above every other, felt, nevertheless, that they were thus leaving a hot bed of disorders in the midst of Italy. The difficulty in the choice of a Sovereign to whom to give those provinces, and the rivalry which might bo brought forth by their possession, made the balance preponderate in favour of the Pope ; and Cardinal Gonsalvi obtained, but only after the battle of Waterloo, this unexpec ed concession. The Pontifical Government, at its restoration, took no account of the progress of ideas and the profound changes that the French regime had introduced in this part of its States. From this a struggle between the Government and the people was inevetable. The Legations have been the prey of an agitation more or less secret, but which at any opportunity may break out into revolution. Three times Austria intervened with her armies to re-establish the authority of the Pope, constantly repudiated by his subjects. France replied on the second Austrian intervention by the occupation of Alcona, on the third by the taking of Rome. Every time that France has found herself in presence of such events, she has felt the neces-

sity of moderating this state of tilings, which is a scandal for Europe and an immense obstacle to the pacification ofltaiy. The þÿ þÿMemorandum of 1831 proves the deplorable state of the country, and the necessity of administrative reform. The diplomatic correspondence of Gaeta and þÿl ortici carry the impression of the same ieeling. The reforms which Pius IX. himself initiated in' 1 846 were the fruits of his long sojourn at Imola where he could judge witli his own eyes of the effects of the deplorable regime imposed on those provinces. Unfortunately, the counsels of the Powers, and the good intentions of the Pope, were destroyed by the obstacles which the clerical organisation opposed to any species of innovation whatever. If there is one fact thatisclear from the history of latter years, it is the difficulty, or we should rather say the impossibility, of reform by the Pontifical Government responding to the wants of the time and the reasonable desires of the population. The Emperor Napoleon III., with that true and firm coup þÿd oeilwhich is his characteristic, has perfectly affirmed and clearly indicated in his letter to Colonel Ncy the solution of this problem þÿ Secularisation and the Code þÿNapoleon. But it is evident that the Court of Rome will combat to the last extremity, and with all the means in its power, the execution of these two designs. It well knows how to accommodate itself bv apparently accepting civil and even political reforms, sure of rendering them illusory in practice; but it also sees that

secularisation and the Code Napoleon introduced into Rome itself, where the edifice of its temporal power has its foundations, would bare it to the roots, and cause it to fall, by cutting away the principal support þÿ clerical privileges and canonical þÿrights. Nevertheless, if it cannot be hoped to introduce a true reform exactly in that centre where the union of the temporal authority with spiritual power is so interlaced that it is impossible todisconnectthem wihout running the risk of destroying them, itmay at least be realised in those parts which show themselves less resigned to the clerical yoke, which is a burning torch of turbulence and corruption, which furnishes a pretext for the permanent occupation of the Austrians, excites diplomatic complications, and disturbs the European equilibrium. We are of opinion that it is possible, but on the condition of separating, at least administratively, those parts from the State of Rome. In such manner an apostolic principality would be formed of the Legations, under the high dominion of the l'ope, but ruled by its own laws, having its own tribunals, finance, and army. We consider that renewing as much as possible that order of the traditions of the Napoleonic kingdom will he sure to produce soon a considerable moral effect, and will be a grent step towards re-establishing tranquility among those populations. Without llattering ourselves that combinations of this nature can last eternally, wo consider, however, that for a long time

it woelil be sufficient for the end proposed to pacify those provinces, and give satisfaction to the wants of the people, and thereby assure the temporal Government of the Holy Sec wihout the aid of a permanent foreign occupation. Wo will indicate briefly the essential points of the project, and the means of giving them eft'ect. 1 . Nevertheless the diplomatic and religious relations will remain exclusively the concern of the court of Rome. 2. The territorial and administrative organisation of this principality to bo established in the form in which it was under the reign ol Napoleon I. until 1811. Flic Code Napoleon to be promulgated, except the necessary modifications in the titles regarding the relations between Church and State. 3. A lay pontifical vicar to govern these provinces, with ministers and a council of state. The position

of the vicar named by the Pope to be guaranteed for ten years at least. The ministers, the counsellors of state, and all the governmennt officers, to be named by the pontifical vicar. Their legislative and executive powers never would extend to religious matters, nor to mixed matters that will be previously determined, nor in tine to whatsoever regards political international relations. 4. These provinces to contribute a fair proportion to tlm maintenance of the Court of Rome and to the'service ot the public debt actually existing. 5. Washington, May 15, 1856. As I predicted, the President communicated to the Senate to-day a message upon the Central American imbroglio. He meets the question squarely and boldly. The documents accompanying it are very voluminous, including the entire correspondence up to this time respecting the difficulties between our government and Nicaragua. It created considerable excitement about the Capital, and a very animated debate sprung up in the Senate between Messrs. Crittenden, Mason, and Weller. It will be continued to-morrow. Captain Sands, of the Navy, who has been ordered to Nicaragua, left here this evening, with important despatches to our Minister there. He was closeted a long time with the Secretary of the Navy before he left. He will proceed without delay. Yesterday afternoon Secretary Marcy sent for Mr. Marcoleta, ex-Minister from Nicaragua, as an act of courtesy and informed him of the determination of the administration to receive Padre Vijil as Minister from Nicaragua. Mr. Marcoleta complained of it as violative of the law of God and the law of nations. He entered his solemn protest against the proceeding, and informed Mr. Marcy that he should prepare an expose of all the facts, to be communicated by him to the members of the diplomatic corps resident near this government. Quite a number of Senators are of opinion þÿ among them Mr. Clayton þÿ that we are on the eve of a war with England. Indeed, a universal impression prevails here, in well informed circles, to that

effect, and that nothing can avert it but a change in her offensive and aggressive conduct towards us. If she persist in her interference in Central American affairs, and the stoppage of our merchant vessels, there is no doubt the administration has determined at all hazards to resent it ; and this determination is all the more important as it is the result of outside pressure by distinguished men in Congress which cannot longer be resisted. The bold and prompt avowal of Senator Douglas in favor of the immediate recognition of Nicaragua forced the President into that course. Mr. Crampton will speedily receive his passports. The President declares that the only reason he did not dismiss him long since was the desire to wait for the reply of the British government to the demand for M r. þÿCrampton recall, s so as not to be obnoxious to the charge of want of due courtesy.

SPEECH OF HIS EXCELLENCY GOVERNOR SCHLEGEL INTRODUCTORY TO THE DRAFT OF A LAW REGARD- ING THE REGULATION OF THE POSITION OF DEN MARK TO THE DANISH WEST INDIES. delivered at the 6th meeting of the third session of the Colonial Council, Thursday, Sth of May, iris.) (Continued from our last.) " It was observed that the legislation of the Islands is Danish ; that, considering the principles, according to which they have always been administered, it would be more in the spirit of times gone by, that the Administration be conferred upon the Ministries of Denmark proper, and that the influence on the colonial Legislation inherent in the Diet according to the Colonial Law, which is partly of a legislative, partly of a mere controlling nature, in as far as the King exercises the legislative power, especially with regard to the extension of Danish Laws to the Colony, would be more effectual in the hands of the Danish Diet than in those of the Imperial State Council. The opposition which the Law Draft met with induced the Minister to join a proposition that was made of appointing a Committee to report on the means of regulating the matter in conformity with the Proclamation regarding the limitations of the Fundamental Law, so that it could be determined, which are to be considered the interior affairs of the Colony and what should be, in a financial point of view, the consequences of their being placed under the Diet ? The Report of this Committee, which may with justice be considered as the basis of the present Law Draft

and the necessary elucidating documents attached to it, without which it would remain unintelligible, are so extensive, that the translating and printing it would have too long delayed its presentation to the Assembly. I shall therefore in lieu try to give a sufficient sketch of its oontents for the information of the honorable Members. " First of all the proposition of the Ministry, to rank the interior affairs of the Colony among
roix TRYKT DO UDGIVET AF E N K E-M ADAM E H A R It I E T II A T C H E T 'I'.

CHRISTIANSTED, TIRSDAGEN, deu 1 7de JUNI, 1 8 5 6. the general affairs of the Monarchy, is objected to by the Committee, who say that there in the quiet, ordinary course of things is no necessity to give over all the affairs of the Colony to one single Minister, but that a preferable arrangement might be effected by laying the whole of them into the hands of those Ministers, to whom the management of the corresponding affairs of the Kingdom is intrusted. No such affairs regarding the other parts of the Monarchy are delegated to the Imperial State Council, which would after the ministerial Law Draft be the case in respect to the Colony, and it could be apprehended that the importance of the affairs for the trade and the finances of the Mother Country might weigh heavier with the Imperial State Council than the intrinsic merits of the matters themselves and their interest for the Colony. The popular influence upon the interior affairs of the Colony would also be lessened by placing them in the hands of the Imperial State Council, and the furtherance of reforms would be much more facilitated by the unlimited power of granting pecuniary aid inherent in the Diet than by a the Imperial State Council, tied down as it is to " Normal Budget." " It has ultimately been remarked, that the inhabitants of these Islands live under the Danish Law, and have for a long number of years experienced the influence of the development of the judiciary system and the juridical institutions of the Mother Country, but these historical traditions are more likely to be permanently pre-

served when the interior affairs remain under a purely Danish Legislation and Administration. The Committee therefore deemed proper to recommend : that the " Folkething" should acquiesce in the principle laid down at the limitation of the Fundamental Law, and endeavoured to come to a preliminary agreement with the Government, that might in time serve as the basis of a final settlement, which of course would require the co-operation and concurrence of the Imperial State Council. " The question, which affairs were to be considered as interior affairs of the Colony was so far settled, as the Government, although adhering to its original view of the matter, that a division of the Administration, Legislation and Finances of the Colony was not advisable, agreed, such a division being once resolved upon, to define the interior affairs of the Colony as corresponding with those which by the limitation of the Fundamental Law were designated as being the separate affairs of the Kingdom. The most important of them, as far as they can bo applied to the Colony, are : " The Department of Justice and Police, including the ordinary Legislation on civil and criminal affairs and the forms of judicial proceedings þÿ 1 he Church and School Department þÿ Municipal affairs þÿ The support of the poor þÿ The relations of trade and professions þÿ The affairs of landed properties in the country and the general agricultural matters (Landkasen) þÿ Taxation of real property, income and trade and business þÿ

Stamp dues þÿ All revenues and expenditures connected with the separate affairs þÿ Every new separate tax and contracted public obligation þÿ The Department of publio Health, of the Harbours, j Mother Country, the higher local Administration, Roads, Insurances, Right to stranded þÿgoods the Officials belonging to the Administration in

V A vis. 1 4 9 . Militia, public and charitable institutions and foundations, Fiefs and Entails. " 'Ihese then were to be considered as the separate, the interior or exclusive affairs of the Colony, the Administration of which was to be laid under the respective Danish Ministries and the legislative power on which belonged to the Diet, with due regard, of course, to the Colonial Law. I he Report of the Committee expresses the opinion that it would be desirable that the Colony should gradually under ample development of the Colonial Council acquire the full influence on the final settlement of these matters, but must consider it unadvisable for the present, on account of the incongruity of elements in the composition of the population in a Colony where slave-emancipation has taken place only a few years ago. " The financial side of the question is considered in the same light by the Committee : from a financial point of view the Kingdom ought to derive neither profit nor loss from the influence which it will exercise on the separate affairs of the Colony ; consequently, if the separate Colonial Budget shows a surplus, the Colony itself should benefit by it, if it shows an Under-Balance, that should be paid by the Colony, as far as tho Monarchy might not be incliued to grant an assistance." It is the Monarchy, and not the Kingdom, as a separate part of the realm, which has derived and will henceforth continue to derive all the advantages accruing from the possession of the Colony.

" It is from the financial point that the greatest difficulties in this matter spring ; nor did the C ommittce succeed in coming to an understanding with the Government in this respect. " It was considered self-evident, that the separation of Legislation and Administration must he followed up by a corresponding division of the colonial Budget into a general and a special one, and the Committed is of opinion, that such a division, if based upon the distribution hitherto observed in tho colonial Budget, will be effected thus, that the following three posts be entered as General Revenues: I, Customs and Ship Dues ; 2, Fort Dues ; and 3, Post Revenues ; all other items to be considered as special, with the reservation however, that under the heads " Fees for Patents of Nomination" and " Sundry Revenues" some might be inserted which, according to their nature, ought to he posted among the General Revenues. Of the Expenses the Committee consider the following as special : 1, The Upper Court ; 2, The Department of Justice and Police ; 3, The Clergy ; 4, The Pilot and Harbor Department; 5, Institutions of safety in the Harbours; 6, The Judge and Pliysiciau in St. Jan ; 7, The Public Sohools and Missionary Department, þÿ all the remaining Expenses to be considered as general. " On the part of the Government it has been urged, that among tho Expenses which by the Committee have been put down as general, there are some which concern the special affairs of the Colony just as much as the general State E
penses. This may be especially said of the penses, and thus constitute a class of mixed Ex- . 1lowing : The Superior Administration in at

St. Croix as well as in St. Thomas, the Maintenance of invalid negroes, the keeping buildings besides the military ones and the Custom Houses in repairs, uncertain Expenses, the establishment of a steam-communication between the Islands and finally the Inspector of the West India store-house in Copenhagen. These mixed Expenses the Central Administration of the Colony proposes to be divided between the general and the special Budget after the same ratio as the Bevenues are divided, viz., as 10: 29 or abou thus, that i formed the special, and the general Expenses ; the Minister of Finances has on the contrary insisted upon their being equally divided between the two Budgets. " The Ministry has drawn up a preliminary Budget for the financial year 1856 þÿ 57, in which the Revenues are estimated at $294,128 and the Expenses at $292,575 15cts., showing a surplus of $1,552 85 cts. " A division into a separate and a general Budget shows the following results : " The Revenues will, when Customs and Ship Dues, Fort Dues and Post- Revenues are reckoned as general, and all the rest as special Revenues, will amount : The general Revenues to $219,035, the special Revenues to $75,093. " The Expenses will, according to the proposition of the Committee (without any reference to the so-oalled mixed ones, hut these being posted among the special) amount : The general Expenses to $225,710 27 cts., the special Expenses to $66,864 88 cts., consequently the general Budget would show a minus of $6,675

27 cts., the special Budget on the contrary a surplus of $8,228 12 cts. " When the division is effected in accordance with the proposition of the Director of the Colonial Department (the mixed Expenses being divided after the ratio of 10 : 29) the general Expenses will amount to $208,996 68 cts., the special Expenses to $83,578 47 cts. The General Budget would accordingly show a surplus of $10,038 32 cts., the special Budget a minus of $8,485 47 cts. " Lastly, when the mixed Expenses, in conformity with the proposition of the Minister of Finances, are divided into two equal halves, the general Expenses would amount to $ 188,1 18 77, the special Expenses to $104,456 38, and the result of the Budget would be, a surplus in the general Budget of $30,916 23 cts., and a minus in the special Budget of $29,363 38 cts. Viewing the following article as one of some interest to our Agriculturists, con- nected as it is with the " Imphee," the plant offered as a rival of the far-famed Sugar-cane, we beg to draw attention to the fact, that, although there has been no success attained in the imperfect experiments made here, as well as in British Guiana, yet sanguinary hopes are entertained as to its final success upon a fair trial : þÿ THE HOLCUS SACCHARATUS. About three months ago, some 28 seeds ' of the above plant were given to Mr. Henry, the Manager of plantation "La Penitance," for the purpose of testing the capability of the sweet reed, as a sugar producing plant. The plants grown from these seeds were cut on the 20t,h instant, and yielded 5 imperial pints of juice. Mr. Henry says that he boiled this in a saucepan, to the consistency of the sample sent to us, and obtained five imperial half-gills. It will readily be seen that with such a small quantity of liquor and with such rude appliances, no accuracy in the boiling and tempering could be obtained þÿ consequently the juice was burnt in the process ; and too much

temper lime having been used, the granulation is far from complete, indeed lost. The density of the juice was, Mr. Henry reports, " about equal to that given by the canes on La Penitance," when they are fully ripe. The reeds were pounded in a mortar, and squeezed through a piece of coarse oznaburgh, and this was sufficient, Mr. Henry thinks, to prevent granulation. Judging from this yield, the produce per acre would only amount to 500 lbs. imperial of sugar ; hut this, it is submitted, cannot be a criterion, as the weather has been very unfavourable to the growth of the plant, and it is not even certain, that all was got from the experimental seeds, which under a superior process, might have been obtained. The quantity of seed obtained from the original twenty-eight, is about equal to five imperial pints, " an immense return." Mr. Henry's opinion is on the whole favourable, and he thinks that this sweet reed will furnish a " wholesome food" both " for man and beast." Though this experiment has not entirely succeeded, yet it has furnished returns favourable to further investigations, and we have no doubt that with a greater quantity of juice, and better machinery, it will be found, that this plant is not undeserving the attention of agriculturists. Mr. Henry, as soon as the weather permits, will sow a greater quantity of seed, and, in all probability, his perseverance perfect result. þÿ " Guiana will lead to a more Colonist."

EUROPEAN EXTRACTS. (From the London Times, May 13, 1856.) Our readers are now in possession of the Note addressed bv the Plenipotentiaries of Sardinia to the Paris Conference. Its contents have been aleady in a great measure anticipated by the conversations reported in the 22nd Protocol, but still it is impossible to peruse such a document without feelings of the liveliest interest and sympathy. The Plenipotentiaries begin by stating þÿth they t were disappointed in the hope that the Congress would not separate without taking into consideration some plan for restoring the equilibrium of Italy, now disturbed by forejgn intervention, although they admit at the same time that, owing to the peculiar position of Austria, such consideration turned out to he impossible. They therefore introduce the suhject on their own account. The evils f Italy they attribute to foreign intervention, and the system of repression, which was justifiable perhaps in 1848, has been persevered '"!? for eight years with unremitting or even increas- ot affairs is fraught with a double danger for Pied- rigour. They state that the condition mont, þÿ first, the awakening of revolutionary passions, from which the temperate and balanced liberty of a limited monarchy has al most as much to dread as absolutism itself ; and, secondly, from the measures which Austria ' suit of which is that, she envelopes with a large takes with the view or under the pretence of counteracting revolutionary movements, there

force the eastern frontier ot Piedmont, occupies Parma, fortifies Piacenza, and thus obliges her weaker neighbour to maintain an amount of force which drains her population, and is ex tremely injurious to her straitened finances. Sardinia, they remark with much truth, is the only State in Italy which has been able at the same time to erect a barrier against the revolutionary spirit and to keep free from the insidious and still more perilous protection of Austria. Sardinia has combated anarchy not with despotism, but with moderate and reasonable freedom, and for this reason anarchy and despotism are equally in league against her. Whatever, therefore, promotes the cause of Mazzini or Radetzky þÿ whatever stirs up the passions ot the populace or stimulates the cruelty and ambition of priests or soldiers, the twinborn pests of Italy þÿ is equally dangerous for Piedmont, which, being built upon popular and monarchial principles, has everything to fear, whether from the sword of the despot or the torch of the incendiary. This, then, is the condition of Piedmont, and , this the right on which she claims to bring before assembled Europe the Italian question. She is possessed of an excellent constitution, a enjoyment and preservation of freedom. þÿ patriotic King, and a people well fitted for But the these blessings she is not permitted to enjoy nay, she is threatened every moment with their loss or curtailment, because the pleasure of certain conservative Powers, 011 the one hand,

to stimulate the passions which fill her towns with political exiles and tend to confuse her Government with that of her arbitrary neighbours, while, 011 the other hand, these same Powers are constantly acting with revolutionary violence, and committing, in the name ot order, worse exeessess than anarchy itself could devise or execute. The ground taken by Piedmont is the very one so often used to justify armed intervention þÿ the dread of the mischief which the disturbances of one State may bring to the welfare of another, only here the argument is used to prevent, instead of to further, foreign interference. New York Court of Appears. þÿ The supremejudicial authority in the State of New York has decided that the Prohibitory Liquor Law is unconstitutional, and of necessity the law is at once blotted from the statute-book. The ground of this decision is just what the most sagacious friends of temperance clearly foresaw þÿ viz., that the seizure and ferfeiture clauses were in conflict with that clause of the constitution which declares that " no citizen shall be deprived of his property except by due process of law." It is thought that this decision settles the question virtually for the whole country. It has, at all events, dealt a heavy blow on fanaticism, and hereafter fanatical men will be apt to proceed with more caution in their favourite reforms.

Every day's experience illustrates more and more forcibly the inconveniences and anomalies which attend our present system of diplomocy, and the fallacy of the theory upon which the conduct of our international relations þÿ whether of peace orwarþÿ constitution is that to make war and make peace depends. The to theory ofthe is the exclusive prerogative of the Crown, to be exercised irrespectively of all control or interference on the part ot its subjects. In practice, however, the people, being called upon to supply a tlie means voice have controlling for making war, virtually as to the expediency of the war before it is undertaken, and as to its conduct during all its continuance. The practice further, is that when peace is made, or so soon after as the cumbrous and delatory forms of "ratification" have been gone through, the Crown informs its subjects of the fact, by messages to both Houses of Parliament, and by proclamation to the sound of trumpets; and calls upon the country to offer up thanksgiving, and to rejoice amid the blaze of fireworks and illuminations. Both in the case of war and peace, therefore, the Royal prerogative defers to the popular opinion ; but with a difference. In the initiating and throughout the conduct of war the popular will possesses the power ol a direct veto upon the, exercise of the Royal prerogative, inasmuch as the supplies must be of its giving ; on the contrary, when peace is to he made, the Royal prerogative is free to act

unchecked by the popular will, inasmuch as the Crown has no need to call tor additional grants of money to effect its purpose. What is the result? That the country is called upon publicly to sanction and to support a war the issues of which are to be regulated privately and irresponsibly by the Royal prerogative þÿ to carry on a contest at great expense of blood and treasure, having approved the purposes with which it was undertaken, but without the faintest pretence at a voice in adjusting the conditions up on which it may be terminated. A precisely unlimited means to conduct suit who should parallel case would be that of a giving a solicitor have authority to compromise it at any moment upon terms that might not be to the interest ot his client. Secret diplomacy, the bane and curse of all international relations, is a relic of the ancient theory of absolute monarchy, which admitted of no will, no interests, in the State but those of the Sovereign. Tins theory, we all know, has long been exploded in this country, and therefore, while secret diplomacy may still be very applicable to despotic States, where there is onl) one will to consult and satisfy, it is both absurd and hurtful in a constitutional State, where the ultimate power and charge rest with the, people. In the United States of America and other Republics this anomaly does not. exist In such Governments the sanction of all deplo matic relations is with the Senate, or representative body ; and, consequently, secret diplo-
macy is impossible among them

The undersigned Committee, elected by the Colonial Council to report on a proposition presented hy the 2nd Member for Christiansted District that the passage in 25 of the Colonial Law : þÿ The meetings of the Council are not þÿpublic should be changed to þÿ The meetings of the Council are þÿpublic have in due appreciation of the decisive importance of the question at issue submitted the proposition to
St. Croix Avis. TRYKT OG UDGIVET AF ENK E-M ADAME HARRIET HATCHETT

CHRISTIANSTED, TIRSDAGEN, den 2 4de their most careful and minute examination, proceeding from the reflection, that the aim and end to be attained by the establishment of the Colonial Council must be, by degrees to capacitate the population of these Islands for a beneficial and invigorating public life, and to build the future of the Colony upon the firm foundation of liberal institutions and a j free cooperation in the. legislation on its own most vital affairs and interests. The Colonial Council stands near the end of ' its third session. Its action has been extensive, 1 it has had to report on the most momentous i legislative matters, and the Members have had ample time and opportunity, as well to familiarize themselves with the forms of Parliamen tary Debate, as also to acquire the expanded and comprehensive view which is required for the treatment of general and public nftairs. We are therefore of opinion, that a progress in the direction pointed out by the proposition can no longer dispensed with, neither in the in- be terest of the Council, which is in want of an enlivening influence, nor in that of the public, who with justice complain, that they are all hut debarred from a due knowledge of the Proceedings, in as much as on account of the absence of the means and auxiliaries generally at the disposal of such Assemblies for the exact and minute publication of their Debates, the Extracts from them must be too brief and succint to afford to the electors a real insight into the activity of their representatives, in which

respect we will add, that the intended publicity of the meetings, limited as it be, would enable the press, through the medium of reporters to publish the very details of the discussions, and would thereby form a useful substitute of the free press, which from a variety of external ns well as internal reasons has not yet been introduced. Whilst we deem it superfluous to adduce ulterior arguments in support of our conviction, which is based, partly upon general principles, partly upon special experience and observations we have not neglected well to weigh the formal and material limitations in the realization of this plan, which the particular local circumstances render indispensable. Above all a paramount regard is due to His Excellency the Governor, in regard to the use of the locality. On the other band the dignity of the Council demands certain modifications, which, we think, flow very naturally from the leading principle, that there can merely be a question of a gradual extension of constitutional institutions, or in other words, of a measure conducive to the formation of a strong and sound public opinion ns the basis of the future political developement of the Colonies, and in this respect we the more confidently count upon the approbation and support of the Home Government, as the consultative provincial Diet of the Ducliy of Sleswig, originally not public, has recently obtained publicity, in virtue of the Ordinance of the 15th February 1854. On the strength of this position, and consi-
dering the actual state of the institution, guided also by 23 of the said Ordinance, the committee propose unanimously :

The following is from the þÿ Bombay Overland þÿTimes : þÿ On the 6th and 7th May, a succession of shocks of earthquake was experienced over nearly the whole of the Punjaub, and so on to Simla ; the mischief occasioned by them does not seem to have been at all considerable. The Northern portion of the Punjaub is one ol our great centres of earthquake, and though there is no appearance of an active volcano having during the human period manifested itself within a thousand miles of the Indus, seldom a year passes that Peshawur is not shaken. The correspondence of the þÿ Independence þÿBeige at Warsaw gives the following as the substance of a speech addressed by the Emperor Alexander to a deputation of the inhabitants of that city who waited upon his Imperial Majesty on the 23rd : þÿ line of conduct towards My your country is þÿ absolute forgetfulness of the past. I am content with the Poles, not merely because, in spite of revolutions and wars in which all Europe has been entangled, they have not forgotten their duties to their Sovereign and to themselves, but still more because those of them who have fought in the ranks of my soldiers have displayed a bravery and fidelity which have been against all temptation. FACTS AND SCRAPS. Popish Mercy in Verona. A journal þÿ of Malhouse the Lion þÿd ISRAEL, gives the following account of an incident which is commented on in severe terms by the þÿ Siecle : þÿ þÿ very A wealthy Jew, named Pincherlie, inhabits Verona, where his numerous and unostentatious charities procured for him universal esteem. This person possesses an only daughter, who has recently reached her seventh year. he On the ed a letter from the cure of the parish day when he celebrated this event, receiv- in which he resided, stating that his daughter could no longer continue to live with him ; and that she must prepare herself to enter a convent, in order to be brought up in the Catholic religion. The explanation given by the þÿ lows: þÿ When your daughter was two cure for this demand wras as folþÿyears old she was extremely ill; her nurse, who was a Catholic, in order to save her soul, baptised her in the room, without witnesses. According to the Catholic religion and the Austrian laws, the baptism is perfect and binding, and you have no right, as a Jew, to keep a Catholic child in your Owing to the personal influence of the father, and the present state of political matters in Lombardy, the father and child were permitted to take exile in Turin. A touching scene then occurred. Many persons of high standing in Verona, the workmen and servants of M. Pincherlie, all Catholics, waited upon the bishops, and implored him to allow the father to retain possession of his daughter without being

þÿ compelled to exile himself. That prelate, giving way to the prayers of the deputation, consented to this request on two harsh and unacceptable conditions. The girl might remain in the house of her father until the age of 1 4, when she was to choose between the two religions ; the second condition, which rendered the first illusive, was that Catholic priests were to be permitted to instruct her in the hatred of everything that proof love and respect. Will the father accept she had been taught from her childhood to these conditions? Will he consent to purchase the right of residing in Verona at so dear a price ? Can he live under the arm of that savage Austrian law, which menaces the father in his holiest þÿaffections? The following are the comments of the þÿ Siecle þÿ such If are the fruits of the Concordat concluded between Austria and Rome, this Concordat will became the signal of the most terrible misfortunes. Let Austria be aware that she is on the decline which leads nations to their ruin. Her alliance with the two great nations of the West imposes on her duties which she fails to recognise. The time is past when the House of Austria could give to the world the spectacle of abominations, murders, spoliations, which accompanied the re-establishment of Catholicism in her States. The Jew who is to be deprived of his daughter, in the name of Jesus Christ, is in possession of an immense fortune. The anxiety of worldly

goods enters at least as much as the anxiety of souls into the preoccupations of the Catholic clergy of Verona. Can France or England, the allies of Austria, permit such attempts ? This we do not þÿbelieve. þÿ London Weekly Dispatch. Civil Liberty. þÿ Men are qualified for civil liberty in exact proportion to their disposition to put moral chains upon thenown appetites ; in proportion as their love of justice is above their rapacity ; in proportion as their soundness and sobriety of understanding is above their vanity and presumption ; in proportion as they are more disposed to listen to the counsels of the wise and good, in preference to the flattery of knaves. Society cannot exist unless a controlling power upon will and appetite be placed somewhere ; and the less of it there is within, the more there must be without. It is ordained in the eternal constitution of things, that men of intemperate minds cannot be free ; their passions forge their fetters. þÿ Ibid.

Fall of a Suspension-Bridge in Canada. þÿ Yesterday morning (April 30) the sad intelligence reached Quebec that the suspension-bridge over the Montmorenci had given way, and that several lives had been lost. Little credence was at first given to the rumour. There had been statements made before to the effect that the bridge was not to be trusted. People crossed it with terror, it was so shadowy, so light, and so high. Like a mere cobweb, it hung across the chasm over the very brink of the Falls. The superintending engineer had asserted that the structure was safe, and the road trust had taken possession of it. Nevertheless, on the northern bank of the Montmerenci, five of the seven strands of one of the wire cables had previously given way, and the cable had been repaired. There was something wrong. Yesterday morning (April 30), while a man and a woman were crossing in a cart, about eight or half-past-eight þÿo clock, and a lad sixteen years age of was crossing foot, the chain on plates attached to the anchors on the south side of the Montmorenci snapped asunder, the bridge dropped down, throwing all upon it over and down the Falls into the pool, 300 feet below, and which is 38 feet deep, swung itself round over the cataract, and there it hangs now like a ribbon from the two towers on the south side. The roar when the bridge gave way was terrific. The clanking of the iron reverberated like thunder. A Mr. Giroux, who lives a mile off, distinctly heard the noise. The bridge is a complete loss to the turnpike trust.

Nothing stands except the towers, one only of which is injured. A Mr. Cloutier was actually upon the bridge with his horse and þÿ light cart a moment before the accident happened, and, but for bis horse and cart, would, perhaps, now have been in another world. The horse perceived something wrong in stepping upon the bridge, hurriedly backed off again and was scarcely otl when the whole structure fell. The bridge cost .£9000. þÿ Illustrated London News.
