The Sound Dues ! The following paragraph, relating to the Sound Dues, is taken from the New York " Times" : þÿ " Washington, June 15. " Secretary Mnrcy has formally signified to the Danish Minister the purpose of the President not to make a forcible resistance to the collection of the Sound Dues, at Elsinore, for one year from the 14th instant, thus virtually bequeathing this question to the next Administration. Meantime the Dues will he paid under protest."

St. Thomas " Times" supplies the follow- The Southampton correspondent of the ing article on the Sound Dues Question: The official correspondence relative to the Sound Dues lias just been published. It extends from October 1855, to May last. The result of the meeting of the commission assembled at Copenhagen for the consideration of the duos levied at the Sound and the Belts was the proposal of a scheme by M. de Blulime, the Danish Commissioner, according to which Denmark was prepared to accept, as a final settlement of the question, a sum of 35,000,000 rix dollars, or 3,937,500/., of which England would have had to contribute a quota of 10,126,855 rix dollars, or 1,139,271/.. being

about 29 per cent, of the total indemnity to he paid to Denmark. These were declared l»v 51. de Bluhrne to be the very lowest terms that Denmark could accept. The Government of ller 5Iajesty, having duly considered the subject, intimated to 51 r. Buchanan in 5Iarch last that tlie.y could not assent to the principle of the proposed arrangement þÿ viz., to the payment of a gross sum for the extinction of the charge. Her Majesty's Government was not prepared to recommend to Parliament to vote a sum of money for that purpose, nor was it likely that Parliament, especially at this moment, would consent to impose so heavy a burden on the general taxation of the country in order to remove a charge on one particular branch of trade. Her .Majesty's Government, at the same time, expressed an opinion that a solution of the difficulty might be found by commuting the present dues for a tonnage duty to he levied by Denmark, for a given number of years, at the first Baltic port of entry or the last Baltic port of clearance, instead of at Elsinore. There appeared to he no insuperable objection to this arrangement, and it would have this great advantage þÿ that, while the amount of the duty and the number of years for which it should he levied, might he fixed on the principle of an annuity, so as to secure to Denmark a reasonable indemnity for the ultimate extinction of the charge, the present obnoxious stoppage of vessels at Elsinore would be wholly done away with, and the charge would he

borne for a limited number of years by that branch of trade alone upon which the present dues are imposed, instead of falling on the general taxation of the country. This proposal of the English Government was decisively rejected by that of Denmark, which, it is declared, "will meet all the risks which the question involved rather than agree to a measure so impracticable and so inconsistent with their interests and their indisputable rights." On the 9th of 5Iay a protocol was signed at Co penhagen, recording the acceptance of the Danish proposal for the capitulation of the Sound Dues by Russia and Sweden.

Mr. < rampton, who has been for some years past the British Ambassador at Washington, arrived here yesterday in the steam-ship Caþÿ nada, and immediately proceeded to Loudon. It was known by the previous arrival that the American Government had determined to dis miss 51 r. ( rainpton and to revoke the exequn tears ot the British Consuls at New York, Philadelphia, and Cincinnati ; so that the realisation of a fact thus foreshadowed did not produce any extraordinary sensation. The dismissal of these officials has been accompanied by the publication of two despatches, both addressed to the American 5linistcr in London, 5Ir. Dal las, by Mr. Mnrcy, the Secretary of State at Washington. The first of these despatches, which is dated 51ay the 24th, 1856, is exclusively occupied with the Central American

question, and which the second, proposals is dated three days later, is for its settlement ; and entirely devoted to the Enlistment dispute, and contains a history of that business, from the tirst unfortunate attempt to raise recruits 011 the soil of the United States, down to the hour when the American Government put upon Mr. Crampton the indignity of sending him foolish for his presumed complicity in that very away transaction. The belief in this country hitherto has been that the American Government, in stirring rip these questions, was mainly moved by electioneering considerations, and that the President and his Gabinet had sought the quarrel for ends of their own. < >f course, a serious affair like this with the United States was certain to fix attention on the origin of the disputes, and u hen, six or seven weeks back, Loid ( laiendon, ill his despatch of April 30 to Mr. Marcy, went into the subject specifically, and argued the point seriatim, people at home were proud ot their Minister, who was regarded as having made out a most triumphant case, looked at from the British point of view. A strong compliment was extended by some of the American newspapers to this despatch of Lord Clarendon's, for it was said to have "cornered" Mr. Marcy. That was certainly the impression at home, and the reading of this able production could not be without its effect abroad. In the meantime the opinion strengthened that as the American Government were weak in arguments, they would wax stronger in bluster, and

that when the pear was ripe Mr. Crampton would be sent home in a manner the most insulting to the country which lie represented, and the best calculated to provoke a tierce War ! But the despatches of Mr. Marcy have dispelled all these surmises. The American Minister is armed at all points, and the mode in which he entrenches himself behind the tollies and the weaknesses of Mr. Cranipton is most damaging to the diplomatic reputation of that gentleman. From the new tacts which come out in the last of these despatches, it is quite evident that Mr. Crampton has not been ingenuous towards his own superior, Lord Clarendon, þÿ has supplied him only with ex-parte statements, which are knocked on the bead by the publication of the actualities ot the case ; and, in short, has caused the I oreign Secretary of Great Britain to advance had argu- he ments which he would not have done known all the bearings of this Enlistment business. Coupled with this damaging course ol controversy, expressions of the greatest regard anil respect for the people ami government ol this country are scattered throughout the American Minister's communications, and as an earnest of the sincerity of this feeling, Mr. Dallas is empowered bv his own government to settle the Central American difficulty on the best terms þÿ with or without a reference to arbitration, as the two contracting powers may decide. It was in the nature of things that this "turning of the tables," this new flood ot light thrown on what was previously hidden or

obscure, should have produced a marked change in the public mind, and accordingly we find the leading men in parliament, including Mr. Gladstone, Lord J. Russell, and others, contending that it would lie monstrous folly, a species of insanity, in fact, to dismiss Mr. Dallas, because the Americans have sent home Mr. Crampton, and to quarrel with a country willing and anxious to be our friend, which will not continue to receive a Minister who is proved to have grossly abused bis functions, and who, in a word, was not strong enough for his duties. This is the feeling in Parliament, and a change equally marked appears in the Press þÿ in that portion of it, we mean, which has hitherto taken the highest ground respecting this American imbroglio. If the Government have mnde a mistake in not recalling Mr. Crampton months ago it would only be persisting in error to bolster him up now that his incapacity or something worse is brought out in so painful a light. The American dispute is now narrowed to the solitary point of supporting or abandoning .Mr. Crampton, and the feeling in Parliament, in the Press, and in the Country, þÿ amongst all reflecting men, indeed, leaves no doubt that we must throw overboard an Ambassador who has played tricks grave enough to bring the two greatest maritime powers in the world to the brink of a war. FRANCE. The news from the flooded districts in the South of France is good. Both the Rhone and the Souuo are falling rapidly. The Journal dc I Indre-et-Loire gives the following description ot Tours on Saturday: þÿ "The Rue Royalo presents the appearance of a canal, and boats are plying on it incessantly, carrying relief to the inhabitants, who either would not or could not quit their houses. The Mail is like a torrent, and all sorts of things brought down by the Loire and the Cher are floating about it. Wherever the eye rests, it sees farms submerged, houses that cannot be inhabited lor a long time to come, even if they cau ever be inhabited again, and 011 the heights thousands of victims grouped together without shelter and without food. Even the dark and narrow streets of the old city, occupied by the lower classes, have not escaped. From the Rue Borgne to the commune of La Riche, from the Champ de Mars to the Mail, and from the Place d'Auinont a Saint Souveur, is an immense lake, reaching in height to the first story of the houses. Such is the state of our city after five days of mortal anxiety and indescribable calamities. The accounts from Saumur of the ravages committed by the Loire and the Autliion are even more distressing than those previously received. The pupils of the Cavally-school of that place gave a fine example of courage and devotedness. They plunged into the water with their horses, they saved many invalids and infirm persons from certain death, and compelled the

inhabitants to leave their dwellings. The clergy likewise displayed considerable energy, and effected much iu combating the strauge determination of the people to remain in their houses. A young curate swau to a man who was clinging to a tree, and succeeded in landing him in safety. From Lyons we learn that as the waters recede numerous bodies are discovered, all in a state ot decomposition. A letter from Aries states that the extent of the country inundated in that neighbourhood is at least 20 leagues. Although the waters arc going gradually down, guns are still frequently heard iu different parts round, as signals of distress from the inhabitants of the inundated houses. Boats are moving about iu all directions to render assistance." llis Holiness Pope Pius IX , having learnt the disasters caused by the inuudations in France, desired to aid in the succour of the victims who were affected by them, and has intimated to the Apostolic Nuncio at Paris that he will devote to that purpose the sum of 15,000f.

FACTS AND SCRAPS. James Gordon Bennett of the Herald, has returned to New York, from Paris, and is about to settle down quietly in an up-town place, leaving his establishment to furnish him $75,000 a year to make lile comfortable. þÿ N. Y. paper.

The Hobbs Lock Picked. þÿ The Illion Independent asserts that the Day and Newell Lock, manufactured at New York, commonly known as the þÿ Hobbs þÿlock, has at last been picked by Lynus Yale, jun., of the adjoining village of Newport. It says: þÿ þÿ The exact modus operand! of picking the lock, of course, is not expected to be made known to the public just at present ; but it is sufficient to say that, by a singular and ingenious method, the action of the key upon the curve of the tumblers of the lock is mapped out, from which a wooden key is made, which unlocks and locks the lock, and in all respects operates on it as perfectly as the true key. In this manner the lock was opened in the presence of the cashier of the þÿDairyman s Bank, Newport, N. Y., and of the President of the Port Stanwick Bank, Rome, N. Y. And within a few weeks was so opened a 300 dollar lock on a þÿjeweller s safe, in Wall-street, New York; from all of whom certificates to this effect have been taken. This statement, of course, will astound the world, but it is even þÿtrue.

Accommodation for Married Soldiers. þÿ The authorities at the Horseguards have consented to the married non-commissioned officers and soldiers in barracks being provided with separate accommodation for themselves and families, instead of being quartered in the same rooms with the private soldiers. It is understood that Lord Panmure, who has made the alteration, has ordered separate rooms to be built at Chatham-barracks for married soldiers, and that the sum of £6,000 has been granted for this purpose. þÿ London Paper.

The Turkish Police. þÿ The Turkish Government have offered Omer Pacha the post of commander of the whole gendarmerie of the empire, a post which does not exist now, and will have to be created for the purpose. It is intended to connect this appointment with the complete organization of this force on the French system, and several officers of the French gendarmerie have had interviews with the Seraskier and Omer Pacha to discuss the subject. þÿ Ibid.

Extensive Frauds by Consignees. þÿ It has been discovered that some of the boxes brought by the last West India steamer, purporting to lie filled with gold, contain only lead and shot. The amount of the deficiency at present ascertained is about £9,000. A portion having been sent to Paris, the result was communicated to this side, and an examination on behalf of the consignees at the Bank of England demonstrated the extent of the fraud. The boxes came from the interior of New Granada, and were shipped at Carthagena. þÿ Ibid,

in war, it is our dutyr, as far as we can do so, fairly to put ourselves in the place of our adversary, and to weigh his motives for maintaining his cause. England surrenders her fortunes, yields her rank among nations, abandons the security of her empire, if she cedes to threats direct or implied anything that it behoves her honour to keep. On the other hand to assert one claim which the coolest reason cannot maintain is, in the present state of the world's opinion, as certainly to lower her authority and to encounter the almost certain result of abject reverses. Before we come nearer, then, to entering upon a struggle in which we must either win or perish, suddenly or by tlie gradual process of decline as it may be, it is wise to ponder what the Americans say themselves of the quarrel between us. If there is no need to contend in arms against their pretensions, there is nothing dishonorable, and, therefore, nothing unsafe in peace. If they, with a knowledge that they are in the wrong, are determined to wrest advantages or concessions from our timidity, or if their pretensions are altogether based on such false principles as must eventually involve war in their assertion, it is our duty not to shun or to postpone war. From the London Weekly Dispatch. It is understood in diplomatic circles and at the Foreign-office, that the course recommended by nearly all our contemporaries, of dismissing Mr. Dallas, in retaliation of the dismissal of Mr. Crampton, is quite out of the question. Every Sovereign Power has a dilectus persona. in reference to representatives of other Powers sent to it. Every Ambassador must be formally, personally , approved by the Sovereign to whom he is accredited before he acqu ires the status of a representative of his own Sovereign. He may be dirty, drunken, disrespectful, uncouth; it is right to reserve to Sovereigns a title to object to receive or retain an Ambassador without embroiling the countries. Mr. Crampton, if sent away, will be dismissed on personal grounds, of which, rightly or wrongly, the Washington President is the sole proper judge. If the Queen have a personal objection to Mr. Dallas, she may do so too ; hut the dismissal of Mr. Crampton is not a personal objection to Mr. Dallas, and cannot form a proper reason for it.

New Route to Australia. þÿ On Monday afternoon a meeting was convened by advertisement at the London Tavern, for the purpose of hearing a statement in reference to a new postal and passenger route to Australia. Commander Meriton, of the East India þÿCompany s service, who convened the meeting, informed the gentlemen present (who were only few in number) that he proposed to carry passengers direct from Blackwall to Melbourne, without transfer of luggage or change of berths, and that he would undertake to carry her þÿMajesty mails s to Australia in 49 days. He proposed to stop at the islands of Canary, St. Jago, St. Helena, þÿGraham s Town (from which letters could be forwarded to Port Natal, the Comoro Islands, and the Mauritius). He would then go on to King þÿGeorge s Sound (from which place letters might be forwarded to Western Australia), and thence to Adelaide and Port Philip, from which letters could be forwarded to Tesmania, Sydney, and New Zeeland. While the outward voyage would occupy forty-nine days, the homeward trip would occupy 52 days, making 101 days at sea, the average of the Livorpool and Blackwall ships Being 180 days. By the track he would adopt þÿ the precise nature of which he declines at present to make known þÿ he would make the distance from the South Foreland to Port Philip, 11,864 miles. The gallant Commodore stated that he had been 58 years in command of vessels, that he knew the whole of the route, and that he had a steamer of which he would willingly
take the command, if encouraged to do so, and conclusively prove that he could successfully carry out his proposals.

Utility of Tobacco. þÿ Undpr this heading we find the following in the Outre-Mer : þÿ þÿ So many accusations, more or less well founded, have been directed against the use of tobacco, it is but fair, amid its inconveniences, to cite at least one advantage. One of these uncivilised naturals related that a ship, fragments of which were still visible on the shore, had been driven there by a storm, and her entire crew thrown into the hands of the natives. þÿ And what did you do with þÿthem? asked the Commodore. þÿ Killed þÿthem, was the laconic answer of the savage. þÿ þÿ And what þÿthen? þÿ We eat them; they were þÿgood. þÿ þÿ Did you eat all þÿ? þÿ Yes, all but þÿone. þÿ þÿ And why not that one also þÿ? þÿ Because he smelt too strong of tobacco, and was not good; þÿpah! How to make a Fortune. þÿ Take earnestly hold of life, as capacitated for and destined to a high and noble purpose. Study closely the þÿmind bent s for labour or a profession. Adopt it early, and pursue it steadily, never looking back to the turning furrow, but forward to the new ground that ever remains to be broken. Means and ways are abundant to every þÿman success, s if will and actions are rightly adapted to them. Our rich men and our great men have carved their paths to þÿ principle a principle that cannot fail to fortune, and by this internal reward its votary, if it be resolutely pursued. To sigh or repine over the lack of inheritance, instead of inheritance, is unmanly. Every man should strive to be creator instead of inheritor. He should bequeath instead of borrow The human race, in this respect, want dignity and discipline. They prefer to wield the sword of valorous forefathers to forging their own weapons. This is a mean and ignoble spirit. Let every man be conscious of the pover in him and the Providence over him, and fight his own battles with his own good lance. Let him feel that it is better to earn a crust than to inherit coffers of gold. This spirit of self-nobility, when once learned, every man will discover within Figure himself, under God, the elements and capacities of wealth. He will lie rich, inestimably rich in self-resources, and can lift his face proudly to meet the noblest among men.

FRANCE AND BELGIUM. The organs of the French Government appear to have received instructions to keep the question of the Belgian press before the public attention, and to lose no opportunity of reiterating complaints against þÿ Constitutionnel of Tuesday says : it. Thus the The portion of the Belgian press so justly stigmatised by the protocol of the 8th of May, and which, after the recent debate in the Belgian Chambers, found it prudent to maintain a relative moderation, has not persisted for long in its new course. We learn from Brussels that these incendiary journals publish an appeal to insurrection, addressed to the Italian nation by M. Victor Hugo ; and do not conceal that they are indebted for the communication to M. Mazzini. We have to observe that these appeals to the most evil of passions are not published in clandestine papers, as we stated on a solemn occasion. These journals are printed and distributed like all others ; they have their subscribers þÿ not in great numbers it is true ; they are received in public rooms þÿ not in all, it is equally true, tor in some they have been excluded by the subscribers. Therefore, if these papers are not prosecuted, it is

because the Belgian law on the press is impotent. It is to be hoped, therefore, that the Belgian Government will consider the moment has arrived when it is necessary to demand of the Legislature that strength which is wanting in order to render Belgium really a neutral Power, and not a hotbed of incitement to insurrection and assassination. The name of Mazzini is always used when people are to be frightened into repressive measures, or when Governments requite an excuse for any arbitrary encroachment on a system usually liberal. It may be remarked, therefore, that just at the very juncture >\ ben the .aad of the late Roman Republic is said to be working at Brussels, the Kisorgimentn of Turin of the 30th states that lie has issued a circular to his agents, declaring his intention of withdrawing entirely from politics, and leaving London for New York or some other city of the United States. Mis agent at Turin, Advocate Bettini, has been instructed to sell the property he possesses tit Piedmont. RUSSIA. Letters received bv the Jnr/ependance Beige from Moscow speak of the magnificent preparations made there for the coronation of the Emperor. The ceremonial will be regulated by that which was observed at the coronation of the late Emperor Nicholas ; the changes to be introduced will be owing to the circumstance that the late monarch was only crowned at Moscow as Emperor of All the Russias, and took at Warsaw the royal crown of Poland, whereas the present Emperor Alexander 11., will unite the two solemnities. We are assured, and, as it would appear, upon good grounds, that at this coronation most of the pardons reserved for his subjects, and especially for those of the Polish kingdom, will be proclaimed by his Majesty. It is stated that the question has been mooted of granting a complete amnesty to all political prisoners banished to Siberia, or detained in the. various fortresses of the empire ; moreover of founding a school for medicine and jurisprudence at Warsaw, and of abolishing the fees hitherto exacted upon the passports of foreigners, &e. It is said, too, that the German and Swedish provinces of the Baltic, as indeed all those that have suffered more or less from the war, will receive a large share of the þÿEmperor bounty. s In respect of the recruitment, for instance, and the payment of taxes, every possible mitigation will be granted them for a certain number of years.

From the London Times, June 27. ITALY. The Bishop of Arras has just issued a pastoral letter on the present position of the Roman States. The Bishop lately paid a visit to the Eternal City for several reasons, the principal of which was þÿ to study on the spot itself the social question, and to render an account of that situation, which has been so decried þÿ; and the present letter contains the result of his examination and his study. The venerable Prelate is an optimist of the first class ; he thinks the administration of Rome excellent, j and the people of the Roman States contented and happy. Anything that has been said to the contrary is of course false : þÿ þÿ The attacks (made against the Papal Government) are unjust, and the reproaches false, and those who permit themselves to utter them, when they are not the unreflecting echoes of malevolence, which is, for tin most part, the case, are either blinded by prejudice or deceived by appearances which they do not explain to þÿthemselves. When the Bishop of Arras assumes that all others labour under prejudices it is to be presumed that he considers himself completely free from any bias whatever, and that he is a perfectly impartial judge. He says, en passant as it were, that þÿ The Holy Father has deigned to confer on us the distinguished honour of wearing the pallium, and very recently His Holiness raised our Cathedral Church to the rank of a minor Basilica, and decorated the members of our venerable chapter with a cross which exalts the dignity of their choir þÿcostume.

The pallium is considered a distinguished honour accorded to Bishops only as a mark of particular favour, and sent to Archbishops on their investiture. The Bishop of Arras is naturally very proud of the honour of the pallium, but the prejudiced people of whom he speaks so severely may suspect that it palliates in his eyes anything he may have seen worthy of censure. Be this as it may, his description of the Roman people at the present day is curious from the contrast it presents to almost all other accounts.

A letter from Rome in the Resorgimento of Turin, says : þÿ þÿ A subscription had been opened at Rome to strike and present a medal to Count Cavour, to testify the gratitude of the Romans for the dignified and energetic manner in the which he maintained the cause of Italv at Congress of þÿI aris.The subscription list was soon tilled up, counting among the names many of the Roman nobles. þÿ A deputation of the subscribers waited upon the Marquis Migliorati. the Sardinian Charge d' Affaires at Rome, requesting him to forward to Count Cavour the medal and the address which accompanied it. The Marquis received the deputation with great courtesy, thanked it in the name of Count Cavour, and promised to forward the precious token to him. þÿ The following is the address : þÿ þÿ þÿ Excellency, þÿ When, by signing a treaty, Piedmont joined the western alliance, through your care, we felt internally convinced that so bold a step was commanded by high considerations, and we hoped that it would prove ot service to Italy, for we knew you had the welfare of Italy at heart. þÿ þÿ We followed with anxious affection the movements of the Piedmontese army in the Crimea, and when, bravely fighting, they covered themselves and the llag of Italy with glory, our hearts leaped with joy, and we felt proud of the praise lavished on those brave men because they were Italians. Then, when, in virtue of a right acquired at the price of blood, you took your seat among those who had to decide the destinies of Europe, you knew wor-
thily how to represent not only Piedmont but the whole nation ; and, for the first time in a Congress of the Powers, you brought forward

the sacred name of Italy, loudly protesting in favour of her rights trodden under foot. þÿ Rome, which has faith in the initiative of Piedmont for the regeneration of Italy, ap plauded the efforts made in favour of the common country, and, feeling worthy to aspire to a civil government which by character, form, and political reasons is adapted to the whole country, it breathes the prayer that the means pointed out by diplomatic foresight may hasten the accomplishment of the desires of the citizens of Italy. þÿ þÿ As a lasting mark of this glorious initiative, Rome sends you a medal, to hand down your energetic action to posterity. Accept it, not as a reward equal to your merit, but as a mark of gratitude. þÿ THE ROMANS. þÿ þÿ Rome, June 13, 185(1.' þÿ The medal, which is of gold, of large di lnensious, has on one side the effigy of Count Cavour, and on the other the following inscription þÿ For the defence of the oppressed Italian populations, undertaken at the Congress of Paris of 1856, grateful þÿRome.

French Opinions of British Soldiers. þÿ A correspondent, just from Paris, states that the most striking sight on the Boulevards and in other places of resort is the vast number of French soldiers with the Victoria Crimean medal on their breasts. The men and officers wear it with great pride, and it contrasts nobly vvitli their little hits of orange and yell >w ribbon and small crosses. I asked one man what he would have said if any one had told him five years ago that be would be wearing a British decoration? He answered, "Oh, Monsieur, les Anglais sont nos freres a present, il faut ouhlier le passe. Et voyez vous, e'est bien distinguee cette Victoria!" During my stay, I was one day conversing with a French general on subjects connected with our army and certain contemplated changes. He was a Crimean officer, and lie said "Believe me that your army is the finest in the world. You have little to learn from us. Imitate us as little as possible. All you have to do is to give your officers a better ' education militaire,' and to teach your men in peace time to study the shifts and expedients of war." He told me that this was the universal opinion of French officers. I heard a good arguofficer þÿ ment in favour of the peace from a field " You English don't relish the peace, because you don't think you have do anything. ' Assurez vous' you have done enough, and are in a state now to done wonders with your small army. Alma, Inkerman, and the repulse of sorties speak for you. If you were to

fight for six months more you might do something, and so might we; but it is uncertain. The Russians are well fortified, and in great force. If you and we succeeded we should be in no better position to demand peace than we are now þÿ that is, we could not desire or obtain better terms; and if we failed, there would be disaffection in England, and revolt in France."

The Remains of Sir John Franklin. þÿ A box has been received at the office of the American European Express Company, New York, which contains a portion (perhaps all) of the relics of the unfortunate expedition of Sir John Franklin: þÿ One piece snow shoe, marked Mr. Stanley (the name is cut into the wood with a penknife) ; one piece of cane, apparently bamboo; one piece of wood, part of a boat, with copper binding; one piece of wood, part of a boat, with the word "Erebus" cut into it; two pieces hunting; one piece cordage; one piece leather, the inside of a hackgammon hoard ; one piece metal, the graduated part of a barometer ; one piece ivory, part of a mathematical paraded ruler ; one piece ivory, apparently part of a mathematical instrument. This box was received from the Hudson's Bay House, Lachine, to be forwarded to the Hudson's Bay House in London.

CHOLERA ! þÿ The schooner " Reserve" arrived here on Sunday morning from St. Thomas, and brought the startling and unwelcome report that CHOLERA had reappeared at that Island. Among the private letters received by the schooner, one states that one death had occurred from Cholera ; another mentions that there hail been five cases, two of which proved fatal. Owing to the report of the existence of that Epidemic at St. Thomas, we understand that the authorities here have extended the period of quarantine on vessels arriving thence, but to what definite time we are quite unable to say, seeing that no official communication whatever has been sent to us on the, subject, as was formerly done when sanitary precautionary measures were, in course of adoption. These measures the community have a right to be made acquainted with in the most public manner possible, and this, in our opinion, cannot be more, efficiently and satisfactorily done than through the medium of the Island newspaper. Under present circumstances the Public are left to grope in the dark as it were, and compelled to resort to " hear-say" report for their guidance. The " Vigilant" was despatched yesterday to St. Thomas ; and on her return we trust to hear more cheering tidings.

The Hurricane Season. þÿ Friday next, the 25th instant, being the commencement of our perilous Hurricane Season, the day will be set apart as one of prayer and supplication for our preservation during the season. Let us hope that the day may be observed in a becoming manner, þÿ particularly in the presence of the truly melancholy report from our Sister- Island, St. Thomas 1

The " Charley." The shareholders of the packet-schooner " General von Scholteu" having disposed of her at St. Thomas, have purchased the schooner " Charley" (formerly the Pto. Cabello Packet), and placed her on the line between this place and St. Thomas. The " Charley" is commanded by Capt. A. McGregor, measures 26 J lasts, or about 79 tons, is but few years old, and cost her present owners $6,250. Her superior sailing qualities are too well known to be questioned ; she combines beauty with strength, possesses every accommodation and convenience for passengers, and is acknowledged an excellent sea-boat. She arrived here on Thursday night from St. Thomas, and at noon next day, while at the quarantine ground, saluted, and was replied to with 3 guns from the Fort. We wish the " Charley" all success, and that she may receive the patronage enjoyed by her predecessor, the Scholten." "

From the St. Thomas Times, July 16. The Steamer " Wye." þÿ This vessel is now safely up on the Marine Repairing Slip. She did not, however, get up on Saturday evening as we expected, the detention arising from a stiff breeze blowing at the time, which would have made it difficult to place her in position ; and as the Engineer of the Slip was desirous to avoid mishaps, it was determined to postpone her going up to the following (Sunday) morn ing. But even then a second difficulty pre sented itself, for the tide had gone down eight inches, thereby reducing the draught of water on the cradle. As it was, however, known that at 3 p. m. the tide would return, all parties interested remaiued patiently awaiting the hour, when she was warped to the cradle, the shores drawn close up under her, and the Engine set to work, when she commenced gradually to ascend. It was determined after she was partly up and beyond the chances of accident to wait for the next morning, as the men, officers, &c.. connected with the ship had not known rest from the time of her departure from Guadeloupe. As we predicted, numerous parties have been over to inspect the injuries to her hull, the general opinion being that the "Wye" has proved herself a vessel ot uncommon strength, which, if made of wood, would certainly have gone to pieces. But such is her solidity, that with all her working on the beach there is not a door in her cabins but open and shut freely, nor a pane of glass broken. The Engineers of the Factory are now busily occu-

pied in preparing new plates to replace the injured ones. Colonial Fibres for Manufacturing Purposes. þÿ At a meeting iu the Manchester Townhall on Tuesday evening, Mr. Watts, mayor, presiding, Mr. Young, a director of the recently formed Colonial Fibre Company, and Mr. Sharp, gave some interesting information relative to the attempts which have been made to obtain manufacturing fibres from tropical plants growing in British colonies Mr Sharp said the sheetanchor of the Fibre Company's undertaking was the plantain-tree (musa paradisiaca ), as the co louies iucluded in their charter of British Guiana and Jamaica could furnish 500,000 to 700,000 bales of fibre, each bale being about 3cwt In those two colonies this tree was universally cultivated, its fruit being there the chief article of food. Each tree, on arriving at perfection, bore from 251b. to tiOlb. of fruit, and was then left to rot, as it never produced fruit again. It was propagated by suckers, and did not require renewal for 12 or 15 years. The concentric rings of the outer part of its truDk formed one mass of fibre, nnd fibres could he obtained even to the end of the midrif of the loaf. It would be exported in the form of bundles of fibre. Mr. Sharp described the process of converting this tree into fibre, and exhibited bunches of it ; also pointing to fibres obtained from the leaf of the American aloe, and to a much finer and different quality from the aloe variegata. These fibres were adapted to various textile purposes, one of the fabrics being ot the character of silk, but in

some respects superior and worth 3d. to 4d. per lb. Fine paper could be obtained from the fibre, and the mucilaginous centre of the plant yielded a material not unlike cotton. Mr. iSharpe said from these materials could bo obtained articles from the fineness of French cambric to the strength and thickness of a cable The fibre could be dyed, and iu this country would sell at not exceeding 2d. per lb , allowing a large profit. It was further stated that cloth could be manufactured from a mixture of fibre and wool; and that the plantain fibre, though somewhat inferior in strength to Russian hemp, resisted much better the action of salt water. While, on the average, an acre yielded 4cwt. of cotton, 6cwt. of flax, or 7ewt. of hemp, it yielded 48cwt. of plantain fibre, and there were manifest advantages from the plantain being perennial. In British Guiaua, especially Demerara, the company had been offered nearly a million ready grown plants at 2d. each; but iu Jamaica, where thero was neither railway nor river, the company must cultivate for themselves. Russian Property in Balaclava. þÿ The quantity of property recovered by the Russians in plate and money from the ruins of Balaclava and its environs is greater than could have been supposed. The Chief Priest of Balaclava has succeeded in finding a quantity of church plate and silver spoons, forks, jewellery, and pearls, which were hidden in a well that was choked up with butcher's offal. The pearls alone were discoloured. Another Russian waited on Colonel Harding, the Commandant of Balaclava, and requested leave to look for some things he had let t in his house; and, on receiving it, he entered the half-ruined mansion, and removing the stone window-sill, behold ! there was an iron box full of gold and silver, which, he i.iformcd the Commandant, was the portion of his daughter, who was just about to be married. He said he could not trust his wife, and so he had hidden the money lest she shoulJ make away with it, and he was delighted beyond measure when he got permission to take away his treasure as soon as he had proved his right to it. þÿ Inciter from the Camp, June. 10

rrorn tho Loudon Times- June 27, THE SLAVERY QUESTION. The slavery question is the great difficulty of the United States This has been so long and so often said, the United States still keeping together and continuing to flourish, that people have got to doubt whether it is a difficulty. But, though the United States grow in wealth and population every year, this is not all that is wanted for the prosperity of a country. There should be something like peace and harmony among the members of a State. We say, something like it ; complete harmony is, we are aware, impossible ; but, if people cannot agree, they can at any rate agree to differ. But this is just the misfortune under which the United States labour. The slavery question is one on which people will not agree to differ. It is a question whicli appeals to the natural sense of justice and right and wrong, to the deepest instincts and the strongest feelings of the humam mind. People are too serious about it and too much in earnest to be able to treat it as a neutral question. It excites their enthusiasm, and you cannot put down genuine natural enthusiasm. One-half of the population of the United States thinks the other half foes to humanity and monsters in human shape. The other half retorts by the epithets " fanatic," " nigger-worshipper," " meddler," " fool," and does not always confine itself to epithets, as witness the late scene in the Senate-house at Washington. This is the price that the United States pay for their continuance of slavery. Nor can we

say that it is a wholly unjust one. We know the serious obstacles to abolition, and we will not judge them harshly. Still, slavery, in this age, is a deep blot upon any country. However congenial it may have been with former states of society and of the human mind, slavery is repugnant to the enlightened moral sense ; it has become in a later age of truth and knowledge a sin. We cannot think it right that one man should belong to another. It is against the light of reason as improved by Christianity. A nation, then, must expect to pay for setting itself against light, and harbouring the unclean thing. And this is the penalty strife and þÿ hatred, every man's hand against his brother, the bludgeon, the bowie-knife, and the rifle. As long as the world lasts people will fight for justice and truth, or what they think so. You may talk to them about political necessity, but no doctrine of political necessity will reconcile people to what vitally infringes upon their sense of justice and right. If you will, then, have slavery you must fight for it. Human nature will not let you have it without fighting. You are, in fact, by your very position, in a state of siege. This is your punishment þÿ a punishment which comes upon you not by any miracle or extraordinary interposition, but by the natural order of events. In these last remarks we have had in our eye the present state of Kansas. The slavery question, preying, as it does always, like a chronic disease, upon the body politic of the

United States, has broken out just now into a terrible sore and ulcer. The newly formed State of Kansas, on the extreme West, which takes its name from the river Kansas, one of the tributaries of the Missouri, was at its incorporation a free, or non-slave, State. This is the tenderest question which attaches to the first incorporation of a State þÿ " Shall it be a " free or a slave State V The eastern border neighbours of Kansas, the people of Missouri, took umbrage at " the decision in the case of Kansas," and an armed force crossing the borber took possession of the Government, and, putting down the Kansas Legislature, re-established the State on the. basis of a slave State. The Kansas people resisted, and refused to submit to the jurisdiction of the new courts and officers. This state of confusion and anarchy continued six months, the United States, as Mr. Crittenden complained in the Senate, quietly looking on, and waiting to see which side prevailed. At. last President Pierce, yielding to the urgent entreaties of his Southern friends, and anxious to please the slave States, sent, down a United States force to compel submission to the new Government. And now a regular civil war begins, the Kansas people resisting the Federal forces. The New York journals give the news from Kansas as they would from any theatre of war, and

A IIin r to PioNono. þÿ A thoroughly orthodox Catholic priest, the Abbe Micbon, in a pamphlet, just published, in Paris, which will probably make a great sensation, seriously advocates the expediency of the Pope renouncing all dominion at Koine aud going to Jerusalem, there to reside as the spiritual bead of the church. The Abbe starts with the assumption that the renunciation of the temporal power of the Pope at Home is inevitable. The influence of modern ideas being, as he says, inoperative upon Papal institutions, the progressive element in the Roman nation has become altogether antagonistic to the Pontifical Government. As long as diplomacy, aided by force, choses to sustain the old machinery, it may continue to work, but whenever the foreign troops withdraw from Rome the Papacy will find itself face to face with revolution. The Abbe takes it for granted that whenever the revolution shall make head, the Pope will ho forced to abdicate his temporal power, and he doubts seriously whether alter such an abdication he could maintain his spiritual supremacy at Koine with proper dignity. One city alone, a neutral city out of Italy and out of þÿEurope- namely Jerusalem þÿ would offer every requisite for opening a new and flourishing apostolic era. 'The Cardinals, the Abbe admits, would not like the change of locality, but lie affirms that the plan has been favourably entertained by many European Governments

POZZOLANA. Wo have frequently called attention to this valuable cement, (the only one that withstands seawater) and are glad to learn that its remarkable qualities have been recently tested here. The mixture for testing consists of 1 part lime, 2 parts pozzolana, 1 part clear fresh water sand, and 6 parts broken stoue such as is used iu making roads, using fresh water in mixing aud then putting the mixture into the sea iu abox, where it must remain for tiiree days and then taken up. II it sets and becomes hard the Pozzolana is good. In this way the Pozzolana at Mrs þÿSutherland squarry (which is the most convenient for shipping) has just been tested by (he Civil Engineer Mr. Curtis, and the mixture became so hard as to make it difficult to ho broken. The brig Hope is now taking in a load for Bermuda, where large quantities have been already sent, and we learn from private advices that many loads will be required for the Works of Demcrara. Here then is a simple and cheap cement that can be used lor any sort of work, either above or under water, fresh or salt, and which is far superior to the Roman cement which is imported at a heavy expense, and which quickly loses its power. This island, we believe, is the only one iu the West Indies where the genuine Pozzolana is to be fouud, and no doubt large shipments will be made to places where break-water aud other works requiring a strong cement are in course of erection. þÿ St. Vincent Gazette.

When the report reached this Island not many days ago that CHOLERA had again made its appearance in St. Thomas, we ventured to express a hope that by the return of the schooner þÿ þÿVigilant from that Island þÿ whither she had been despatched in quest of information relative theretoþÿ we would receive intelligence of a satisfactory nature ; but alas, she has been the messenger of the too sad confirmation of that report, þÿ and although the Epidemic has not shewn itself in so virulent a form on this occasion as it did in 1853, we cannot but sympathise with our neighbours in deploring the presence for a moment of a monster of such hedious mein. We learn that up to Tuesday last eleven confirmed cases of Cho lera had been reported, out of which six had resulted in death. Proportionately þÿsma! as the mortality may appear to us, yet when we take into account that the. disease ib in ns infancy, who can foretell what may take place in a week or even a day, if proper measures

are not immediately adopted to stay its progress. We have not heard what is being done here, beyond an extended quarantine on vessels from the infected port, in regard to preventive measures. A strict regard to cleanliness ought to be enforced, and such other precautions as are deemed expedient at this time. With anxious hearts we await further information of the progress or decline of the Epidemic ; and while we may indulge favorable hopes, let us, nevertheless, not lose sight of the danger at our doors.

Since writing the foregoing, we understand that the official account received here from St. Thomas states that the disease made its first appearance on the night of the 17th instant, in Vestergade, a black child being attacked, which died the next morning ; soon after a Tortolian and another child were seized, and thus the distemper has continued to progress, until it has reached Eleven cases. Out of these, Six have died, and Five were under treatment. The þÿKing Physician, s Ur. Pedersen, was of opinion that the disease had not assumed an epidemic character, but was simply sporadic. Still, however, every precaution was offensive being taken to prevent communication with the sick, except what was really necessary ; and no time was lost in burying the dead decently.

Metaphysicians in speculating upon the diverse operations of the human mind, have spoken of man as a microcosm þÿ a little world typifying the outer creation, and epitomising its phenomena. The physiologist, in examining his form and physical endowments, may repeat the expression with a more definite meaning; for he can trace in the single individual a reflex of the forms which people, the laws which regulate, and the elements which compose the entire material world The investigation of the form ot man has made it clear that the skeleton of man, having been fashioned after a certain type, other animals are constructed after the same model, with less elaborate detail and narrower capabilities. The series of created beings radiate from the type of structure which man presents ; and the first link in the laws which control their existence and bind them together in one harmonious chain of life, are attached to this grand human form ; which rises as a central pillar in the wide area of being. The appreciation of the chemical changes which are coincident with the life of man, yields a knowledge of the system of laws which govern the chemistry of the earth. The analysis of the elements which build up the human frame, not only brings into view the close ties of relationship which bind humanity to earth by similitude in composition, but it throws a light upon the physical endowments which we possess ; upon the power which we extend over the creatures of the earth; and upon the privi-

And, from the examination of the chemical constitution of the body, it might be predicated that, to man, has been granted dominion over land and over sea ; that and he is to find in each a feeding-ground ; and that the inhabitants of the one and the products of the other are alike destined to be supplementary to his wants and subservient to his will. The Man of Business. þÿ Energy and determination are not, indeed, the sole indispensable elements of succes. They may he applied to evil as well to good purposes, and, in the hands of the evil disposed, the dishonest and the vicious are the most powerful instruments of wickedness. But all things must he made subject in us to conscience and the Divine law, and then the well-regulated and energetic mind, acting iu obedience to the dictates of elevated religious principles, will he the sure guide to a success worthy of the labour expended on its attainment. This important element in the character of Sir T. F. Buxton manifested itself through life in many ways, often becoming apparent, even iu the most simple and seemingly trivial acts. A few examples may be selected. It began to show itself in him when a mere boy, and appears, indeed, to have been inherited from his mother, and fostered, in no slight degree, by her tuition. It is, indeed, one of those habits of mind which early education may do much to implant in the most unpromising soil. The whole course of his preparations for Parliamentary life illustrated his vigour and perseverance ; in the progress of his public measures he was sometimes put to severe trials, in having to follow his personal jugdment and to adhere to his own purposes, in spite ot the opposition, or, what was far worse, the earnest entreaty of his colleagues and friends. One of the finest moral pictures þÿ the resistance ol the individual against united numbers, the victory ot

personal conviction, selftrust, adherence io the sense of obligation and right over every sort ol' inllnence that could lie brought to hear on inferior affections, may be seen in Sir Fowell þÿBuxton s behaviour iu the House of Commons.

A Great Man. þÿ Every man is great as a man, for he who possesses the power of a soul is a great being, be Ills place in society what it may. lie may be clothed in rags þÿ may be occupied in the lowest business þÿ may make no show þÿ be scarcely known to exist þÿ but lie may be more truly great than those who are commonly so called; for greatness consists of force of soul þÿ that is, in the force of thought, in moral principle and love ; and this may be found in the humblest condition. For the greatest man is he who chooses right with the most invincible resolution þÿ who resists the sorest temptation from within and without þÿ who bears the heaviest burdens þÿcheerfully who is calmest in storms, and most fearless under menaces and frowns þÿ whose reliance on truth, on virtue, and on God, is most unfaltering.

From the Barbados Agricultural Reporter. To the Editors of the Agricultural Reporter.

Gentlemen, þÿ 1 had hnrdh despatched mv letter to you by the last Packet, when 1 received a copy of a small work on Agricultural Chemistry and Manures, by Professor Xesbit, and T have been so much pleased with this volume, that I feel anxious to recommend it strongly to the readers of the " Reporter," as a lucid and condensed exposition of the science of Agriculture, by one who is practically as well as theoretically acquainted with the subject. The few shillings expended in the purchase of the book (published by Longman &: Co.), would be very well invested, but as I cannot feel very confident that many will follow my recommendation, and as considerable time must elapse ere the book would be in circulation in the West Indies, 1 have determined to undertake the task of bringing the work before the notice of Planters, by means of such extracts as may embody the views of the Author, and at the same time add weight to the argument which I endeavoured to urge in my last letter. I shall confine myself to such remarks only as may be necessary for connecting the extracts. Many extracts, however, inav he united without any observation of my own. To avoid perplexities, I shall omit the repetition of inverted commas, distinguishing my own few remarks by brackets. " What, therefore, constitutes manure for the plant, is what the plant derives from the soil and the air, that is to say, every substance which is required to make up a plant is adapted for manure. No matter what the manure is.

or where it comes from, you can trace it back to these sources, the air and the earth. Let me point out to you two facts of considerable importance. The first is that plants in their ordinary natural states, as they are found upon different soils, are adapted to take what they want from the air ; yet when you come to work in an artificial manner fas for juicy canes this cannot be relied on. Now let me here point out to you that without draining it is perfectly absurd to think of fallowing or ploughing with a view to the absorption of materials by the soil from the air. It is a sine qua non, t hat the soil shall he either naturally sufficiently porous for water to descend and the air to en ter, or that it be brought to that state artificially, i. e. by draining. It has been proved by some eminent French Chemists, that the rainwater which falls in the neighbourhood of Paris, contains a quantity of nitric acid and ammonia, which I have estimated to he equal to a dressing of 200 weight of Peruvian Guano, the chief value of which is derived from the nitro gen it contains. If your land, therefore, from not being drained is not porous, and so impervious to this descending rain, this splendid supply of the most valuable of fertilizers, will run oti' on the surface. Only think of the value of the triple or quadruple quantities of rain which falling on our Island soils, run off to the gullies and sucks ! We come now to the preparation of farm yard manure. This is generally formed of all the

vegetable matters lyingabout the farm, together with the dung deposited by stock. Now, whether vegetable matter be disintegrated by spontaneous decomposition, or by passing through animals, the result is the same. 1 hat which passes through animals is richer than ordinary

farm yard dung, because of the greater richness of the food consumed. If you feed an uiimal on straw alone, its excrements will be t o richer as regards manure, than straw de- .omposed in the open air; but when you feed upon seed, as oil cake, which contains four or live times as much nitrogen, and also far more phosphates than straw, the excrements are more valuable than straw. Therefore while you use valuable food because you gain by the conversion of it into llesh or muscle, that which is excreted is also valuable because you use a valuable article to produce it. How unwise then to feed stock with expensive materials, and then to allow it all to be dropt about our poor miserable hill sides called pastures. In the case of farm yard dung you simply return for the production of new vegetables, what formed part of the old. Whatever the process of feeding may be, you will find that the dung is neither more nor less than the materials which once grew 011 the land; materials which, having once had vegetable life, are put 011 t lie ground again to sustain that life. Farm yard dung, as 1 told you before, varies in value according to the substances from which it is made. If you feed with linseed and other strong food, the manure ought not to be exposed to the wet, but should he stacked up ; I was going to say, as you would stack up Barley, or mixed with soil. Some covering should always he over it ; and if that were done properly, calcareous matter being which layers, you could make manure laid on 111 would

act, proportionately, quite as strongly 011 your land as any nitrate of soda which you could use. In this way in fact complete nitre hods are made, and from such beds Napoleon obtained all the nitre he used for making powder in his great wars. Observe that of the constituents of farm yard dung, some are volatile and go into the air, others are soluble in water, passing away with the water if that reaches the manure over abundantly, and t lie least valuable parts of the manure are the least volatile, and the least soluble. Ammonia, one of the most valuable of the constituents of manure, which, in fact, is bought in < i n;iiio after the rate of £00 per ton, is that which is the most volatile, and if manure be over exposed or over heated, the ammonia and as it it an is produced is driven water undue quantity of off into the air; readies the manure, all the soluble materials, and especially the phosphates are washed away, not is like so much green thatch, and what remains more valuable and producing no better results. Only think how exactly we often ensure this deterioration of our manure. With respect to artificial manures, it has heen fullv proved, not only here, but in France and America, and all over the world, that those which contain nitrogen, and those which contain phosphate of lime, are the most valuable and the most necessary, for these are elements which are most largely carried away in the produce of the land. It is therefore on the presence of ammonia and phosphate, of lime

that the value of Guano depends; and when we know the quantity of these articles in any given case, we may form a tolerably correct estimate of the value of that manure. You may reckon the price of ammonia in Guano at 6d per lb., so that, if you have an analysis of your Guano, by dividing the number of lbs. of ammonia per ten by two, you get the value (quoad ammonia) in shillings. Good Guano should contain from l(> to 20 per cent of ammonia, hut the system of adulteration scientifically pursued is frightful. The phosphates are worth Us. Id. per lb. Thus we may estimate the value of the different ingredients in Guano. There is moreover a great difference in the Guanos as imported. Where there is little or 110 rain it is in a state of purity, as on the coast of Peru, hut 011 the Islands to the north and south of the dry latitudes, it is found move or less deteriorated hv water; the soluble materials ate washed out, especially the ammonia. The Saldnnha Bay Guano contains only li or 2 per cent of ammonia, and is only valuable for its phosphate. Even Guano obtained from the same Islands may differ in quality. Those which have been most exposed will lie found to he of less value than those which have been covered up and not subjected to atmospheric action. It is well worth while to consider seriously the effect of the exposure to which we systematically subject our Guano in its application.

S T CROIX AVIS . Recurring to the subject of adulterations. Guano ought not to contain more than l.J to 2 per cent of sand ; there should be at least 20 per cent of phosphate of lime, and from 16 to 17 per cent of ammonia, with a quantity of organic matter Now, Guanos are often sold, containing some 60 to 70 per cent of sand, and with scarcely 1 per cent of ammonia. The ammonia still gives a strong smell, so that it is impossible to detect the genuineness or otherwise of Guano by the smell alone. The adulterating materials, however, are almost always superficially heavier than Guano, therefore a given weight of the genuine article, and of an adulterated one being placed in similar glass tubes, the adulterated will occupy a much smaller space ; this is a good ready criterion, method of knowing what one buys. Of though of course an analysis is the only safe- true guards, the only one is to buy of none but price þÿ thoroughly first-rate houses, and to adulterated, .1 cheap article is inevitably give a fair and that to a very large extent, for it would nut pay to adulterate a little. Lime is the next subject considered, but by far the greatest amount of what is said by Mr. N., is not applicable to our case, because the estimation in which lime is held in England, is si 1 general and so high, that Mr. N. naturallv is most desirous of giving caution against its 0 _ O < , , , » overuse, which we certainly do not require. Still a few sentences may be extended. It lias been supposed that limestone is the

better for being pure carbonate of lime. Such, however, is not the fact ; the admixture of other matters increases the value of a limestone for agricultural purposes. There are in fact no perfectly pure limestones. It isclear that limestones must be the better for any phosphate of lime which hones continuallv putting they contain. As we are and other substances into the soil because they contain phosphate of lime, it is evident that those limestones which contain the largest proportion of the phosphates of lime are the most valuable. One per cent is perhaps the average of phosphates in limestones, but many contain much more ; hut even with one per cent., ten tons of limestone, or five or six of lime, put 011 the land would furnish 200 weight of bone earth per acre, which would be a considerable dressing and benefit the land for a long time. It may be remembered that I obtained some years ago an analysis by Professor Johnsoil, of some Barbados marl, which showed that it was rich in phosphates, owing to which circumstance the Professor pronounced it to be very valuable as a dressing for our caue-tields. It does not seem to make much difference, whether you use, calcareous matter merely in the state of carbonate of litne, or in that of disintegrated chalk, or quicklime itself ; by the absorption of air, this last becomes again a carbonate, and it is to this that in all cases the benefit is referable. The most material point is the solubility of the. limestone applied. Bo it remembered that if a

man lias worked his land down to a low state, if he has been taking crop after crop, without much manure, and then fancies that by liming the land he can bring it back to its original state of fertility, he will find himself mistaken. It is upon newly broken up land that lime tells best. It is my distinct opinion that lime ought to be used on such soils as contain a large amount of organic matter ; and when using it on arable lands never to trust to it alone, but to the use of other manures as well, though not applying them together. I wish it to be understood that without the presence of carbonate of lime in a soil, you can never have the full action of any kind of manure." 1 shall not pursue these extracts further, not only because space is wanting, but because 1 wish that the work itself should be read. There are very few points in it which would require alteration, if it were addressed expressly to us as W. I. Planters, and I think I could not adduce stronger argument in support of my former letter, which was despatched before J had read Mr. Nesbit's book. In point ot fact, however, these things may be more or less forcibly, more or less clearly, put, but they almost may be said to be truisms, and to be universally admitted It is scarcely open to us to ask whether they are applicable to our case, their applicability is universal. Fire burns and water quenches, in the tropics as in the temperate zones Man requires food every

day and so do vegetables. Man uses up a limited supply of food and so do vegetables; to support man you must keep up the supply of food, and so you must in the case of vegetables. Well, that's all homely and trite enough ; but if we are thus to keep up the supply of food for our crops, we must take the necessary means for doing so þÿ we must feed stock so as to obtain manure, or we must multiply and care for vegetable crops especially as manure for our more important crops. In the decomposition of these articles of manure, and still more so with those of a more volatile character, we must guard against the disproportion of the most valuable qualities by over-exposure to the action of the air, and we must no less guard against the inevitable loss by the washing away of the next most valuable set of ingredients, by exposure to heavy falls of water, especially where there is only surface drainage. I presume no one would credit a really faithful calculation of the amount of loss sustained by evaporatiou and washing over the extent of our Island, and the more valuable the manures used, the greater the proportionate loss by these causes. The great manufacturers find it worth their while to gather up and turn to account even the devil's dust and shoddy, which in the times of ignorance were thrown away ; we, surely might well look after the very finest of the raw materials, which we put with much pains and more cost into our mills þÿ the soil. I hope I may not appear to be too importunate,
and with much good-will, I remain, Your obdt. Servant,

There is one punt in the future relations of the two countries on which sufficient attention has not yet been bestowed by the British Government. Whenever the Americans have to appoint an Ambassador to London, they select the very best and most illustrious man at their command. They may not always have the best man for President, but they never fail to send one of their worthiest men to the Court of St. James's. It is the "crack" Embassy þÿ the highest in rank, in honour, and in influence. But the British Government does not return the compliment. The Americans think that an embassy to Washington should be as important to the English people as an embassy Paris, Berlin, Vienna, to or St. Petersburg. But the British Government thinks Washington of less consequence, than Lisbon or Munich. The Americans are right, and the English Government is wrong, in this respect. When we next send an Ambassador to Washington, let a man of acknowledged talent, and of high rank, be selected; and the American people will take it as an earnest of our respect and good will towards them. Nature of Sleep. þÿ It is not uncommon complete and continuous, we have for to hear persons attribute the sleeping of "guilty creatures" to hardness of heart or recklessness. This is an error, referable to ignorance of the nature of sleep, and of the fact that all degrees of excitement in the parts of the brain and spinal marrow, associated with the nerves of the sensitive system, are followed by proportional exhaustion. The only limit to this law is the capability of bearing in those parts. Exhausted by mental excitement, the criminal is often awakened for execution; and the soldier, both by mental and bodily excitement, sleeps by the roaring cannon.

ly : When in health, to swallow only the pulp þÿ when the bowels are costive, and you wish to relax theui, swallow the seeds with the pulp, ejecting the skins. CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 5th AUGUST, 1856. CHOLERA AT ST. THOMAS ! ! !

After being kept in suspense for twelve days, without a word of intelligence from St. Thomas, the anxiety of our community was somewhat relieved by the arrival on Sunday afternoon of the þÿ þÿFly from that Island. We have received tiles of the þÿ þÿTidende of the 19th, 23rd, 26th and 30th July, and from the latter have copied an article giving an account of the mortality from Cholera up to noon of that day. Our contemporary states that the deaths numbered forty-four, with five cases of a mild type under treatment. We, however, learn that up to Saturday the deaths had reached 50. When we call to mind that in 1853 the victims from that scourge of the human race were mowed down to the alarming extent of seventy per diem, we may feel grateful under present circumstances, seeing that from the 18th July þÿ the day on which the disease made its re appearance þÿ to the 2nd of August, a period of two weeks, there have not been as many cases as we had the pain then to chronicle in one single day. Nevertheless, and more particularly as we have up to the present time been providentially preserved from that most awful visitation, it becomes the duty of every good citizen to aid in all precautionary measures that may be adopted to ward off the fell foe

The schooner þÿ Vigilant" arrived here this morning from St. Thomas. By her we learn that there had been five more deaths from þÿC h lera since the accounts received by the þÿ þÿFiy, making a total of fifty-five deaths up to vesteidny (the 4th August.)

From tk9 St. Thomas Times, July 30. An intermission of four days from our past to present issue affords us further experience respecting the Endemic with which we have been assailed. So far as figures could be taken as a result, they would certainly shew discouragingly unless accompanied by explanations. The disproportion of the mortality of Sunday compared with the previous days, arises from the iaciease of patients on the previous Friday and Saturday, when we may reasonably conclude the malady was at its highest and most virulent point. Monday was not unsimilar in character to Sunday. We may therefore say, that whilst death was most busy with us on those days, the health and condition of the town was on the increase and rapidly improving, for there were no new cases taking place. On Tuesday we had four deaths, whilst on Wednesday (this day), we have no mortality at all to chronicle. It will be perceived that from our last there have been twenty-four deaths ; we have not, however, on this occasion, been so happy as to ascertain what proportion of that number is to be ascribed to ordinary diseases, still from all we have heard a fair deduction can be made. The Infirmary, to-day, contains but five cases, all of a mild type, none of which have been there for a lesser period than fortyeight hours. By the foregoing it will be seen that we have reason to congratulate ourselves, for we have no fresh patients nor deaths to announce. Without any pretence of being over sanguine, or daring to tritle with a dispensation of Provi-

dence, we may yet indulge the pleasantry, by saying to our alarmists that their game is up, and, like Othello, þÿ their þÿoccupation s gone." We hope for an indefinite period. Deaths To Saturday, 26th (noon) þÿ þÿ Sunday, 27th 20 12 þÿ Monday, 28th 8 þÿ Tuesday, 29th 4 Wednesday, 30th, to noon O

THE PACKET Packet letters and newspapers were re ceived here on Sunday afternoon by the sloop þÿ þÿFly, which left St. Thomas on Saturday afternoon. Our extracts will place the reader in possession of what little news we can glean from the, European files before us. It was expected in England that, the British Parliament would soon undergo a transition, þÿ arising out of the several defeats lately sustained by Lord þÿPalmerston s Ministry. Willmer & þÿSmith s European Times, of the 17th July, says : þÿ þÿ Lord Palmerston, who rubbed on tolerably well with the present House of Commons during the war, is rapidly outliving his senatorial popularity. In the beginning of the week he succeeded with his Appellate Jurisdiction Bill, although the debating power of the House was clearly against him, and he survived the crushing and unanswerable speech of Sir James Graham only to fall before Mr Raikes Currie, a few nights after, supported as that gentleman was by Mr. Gladstone in a speech subdued, but luminous, which went to the very marrow of the question. When a Prime Minister cannot calculate upon the support of the popular branch of the Legislature throughout an entire night þÿ when some stinging defeat overtakes his Government several times in the course of

one week, he is bound to do one of two things, either to dissolve or to retire. The session is so near a dose that a practised stager like Lord Palmerston is hardly likely to have recourse to the last named alternative ; but it is more than probable that he will be compelled from necessity to adopt the first, so that during the ensuing Autumn we are almost certain to have u general þÿelection.
